entries.title: White Sox GM Chris Getz succeeds, survives at 'grueling' trade deadline
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — Chris Getz had been through two trade deadlines as the White Sox’ general manager, but neither compared to the one he just went through with a first-place team.</p><p>“It is very grueling,” he said Wednesday from a makeshift workout area in the Fenway Park concourse. “I wake up in the middle of the night, I wake up early in the morning, and your mind is going.</p><p>“It’s definitely a stimulating time, but because probably of the lack of sleep and the actual work that it entails, it takes its toll. But you’ve got enough adrenaline to work your way through it. And then, when it’s over, you feel like you’ve been hit by a Mack truck.”</p><p>Getz stood as he spoke in the cramped space with weights and machines protected by black curtains, so he seemed to have recovered enough to keep his balance. And as tired as he was, he felt good about what he and his staff accomplished before the deadline at 5 p.m. Monday.</p><p>The Sox acquired a three-time All-Star starting pitcher in Luis Castillo, a two-time Gold Glove center fielder in Brenton Doyle, a reliable reliever in Huascar Brazoban and a veteran catcher in Joey Bart. They had to part with some quality prospects, but none of their coveted ones.</p><p>“We accomplished our goal,” Getz said. “We got better in the areas that we needed to get better in. We built some depth. We got controllable players. We maintained the top-end talent in our organization. It has been a long road to get where we’re at. We feel very good about the process that we’ve been able to carry out.”</p><p>Some of those good feelings come from feedback from other organizations. Getz said clubs were supportive of the players he acquired and understood what his plan was. It reinforced the relationship-building aspect of trading that Getz said is imperative.</p><p>“So much of this is building a rapport with whomever you’re dealing with,” he said. “It may not be a GM or an assistant GM or a president. Oftentimes, organizations are dividing and conquering because you’re talking about so many different players. You might have someone broker a deal, and you come in late to get something to the finish line.</p><p>“The more that I’m doing this, the more value I put in that. In a world that has become highly objective, highly analytical, there’s a difference between valuing the players and actually getting to the finish line in a negotiation. And it takes a combination of all of those things.”</p><p>Getz said trade talks with other teams begin weeks before the deadline, with clubs explaining what they’re trying to accomplish. He said this deadline was unique in that, with a glut of teams in playoff contention, many still were deciding whether they were buying or selling.</p><p>“So not only are we waiting for that clarity, they’re looking for clarity themselves,” Getz said. “It’s a waiting game: Which direction are you going to go? But most of those teams are planning for different scenarios, in that you earmark certain players that you would have interest in.”</p><p>Even when there is clarity, a deal could be made at the oddest of hours, as was the case with the Mets and Brazoban, the late-looming 36-year-old who’s under club control through 2029, when he’ll be 39.</p><p>That trade went down after midnight Monday morning. Getz said he still was looking for another starting pitcher at the time — he had acquired Castillo from the Mariners on Saturday night — but he wasn’t comfortable giving up what it would’ve cost.</p><p>“So therefore, OK, let’s take a step back, let’s assess other pitching talent that’s out there; in this case Brazo,” he said. “He has control, it’s an upgrade for our bullpen, what we felt like was a fair price for someone of his level. And that’s why we chose to go that path. The timing of it just so happened to be fairly late.”</p><p>Getz said he was open to acquiring rental players, but “it became very clear that our systems just didn’t match up for some of those guys.” And as important as it was to Getz that he not disrupt the chemistry in the clubhouse, it was equally as important that he not trade away the Sox’ top prospects.</p><p>“We wanted to maintain the integrity of that, continue to fuel this organization,” Getz said. “We feel like we’ve done that.</p><p>“So I can sleep well now, not purely because I’m exhausted.”</p><div class="PageListL" entries.title: Portillo’s laying off staff at Oak Brook headquarters
entries.summary: <p>Hot dog chain Portillo’s cut 18% of its corporate staff as it continues a strategic reset amid lower sales across restaurants, the company announced on Wednesday.</p><p>The chain known for Chicago-style hot dogs and Italian beef sandwiches has roughly 140 employees at its Oak Brook headquarters at 2001 Spring Road.</p><p>Portillo’s also cut some field management roles. But its layoffs didn’t affect restaurant workers at its 109 fast casual locations nationwide.</p><p>Portillo’s had about 7,800 workers across the U.S. as of December, according to its 2025 annual report.</p><p>"While never an easy decision, it is imperative that we examine areas of the business where we can operate more efficiently and ensure our resources and future investments are directed at the right priorities. These actions, along with other efficiencies, will support our long-term growth strategy,” CEO Brett Patterson said in a news release.</p><p>Portillo’s made the cuts on July 31, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. There was no announcement yet under the Illinois Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act, but there is often lag time before layoffs appear on the state’s WARN website. Employers must report layoffs of 25 or more full-time employees, under WARN.</p><p>The job cuts will cost Portillo’s about approximately $1.1 million in restructuring charges, according to an SEC filing.</p><p>“There were no restaurant-level team members impacted, and you can expect that Portillo’s will continue to produce the high-quality service and craveable food that our loyal fans and guests have appreciated for the past 63 years,” Portillo’s said in an emailed statement.</p><p>In April, the company raised some menu prices by 2% to cope with inflation. Portillo’s noted higher commodity prices for beef and produce in its second quarter earnings call on Wednesday.</p><p>Portillo’s announced net income fell $2.9 million to $7.2 million in the second quarter. Same-restaurant sales — sales at restaurants open for at least 24 months<b> </b>— decreased 1.2%, or $2.2 million, in the quarter.</p><p>On Tuesday, the company named Kevin Kalicak its chief financial officer, effective Sept. 7. He was most recently Olive Garden’s senior vice president of finance.</p><p>It’s the latest management change at Portillo’s as part of a “strategic reset” announced last fall. Patterson was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/restaurants/2026/02/12/portillos-brett-patterson-ceo" >named CEO</a> in February, after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/work/2025/09/23/portillos-ceo-michael-osanloo-resigns-immediately" >Michael Osanloo</a> resigned from the role in September.</p><p>Portillo’s, launched as a hot dog trailer in 1963, has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/02/24/portillos-slowing-national-expansion-weaker-sales" >scaled back</a> an ambitious national expansion amid flagging sales.</p><p>In 2026, the company opened eight new locations, all in Texas. It plans to open a Downtown restaurant at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/08/portillos-open-michigan-avenue-restaurant" >304 N. Michigan Ave.</a> in the fourth quarter. Portillo’s also expects to open a location in Wrigleyville at 3519 N. entries.title: Man charged in 2021 River North homicide
entries.summary: <p>A man has been charged in the 2021 fatal shooting of a man in River North, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Rashawn Ward, 31, faces a charge of first-degree murder and one count of unlawful use of a weapon by a felon for allegedly possessing a firearm as a convicted felon, police said. He was arrested Tuesday.</p><p>The 33-year-old was standing next to his vehicle about 3:50 a.m. in the 800 block of North Orleans Street Sept. 18, 2021 when Ward, inside a blue SUV, is alleged to have opened fire, police said. The man, shot once in the chest, was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital, where he died. He was later identified as Royal Shorts of Hammond, Ind.</p><p>Ward is due back in court for a detention hearing Thursday, police said.</p>

entries.title: Nothing goes right for White Sox in shutout loss to Red Sox
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — Nothing is going right for the White Sox against the Red Sox, on the mound, in the field and at the plate.</p><p>Sean Burke struggled in the ballpark of his youth, Sam Antonacci made two costly mistakes and the White Sox couldn’t dent Sonny Gray in a 4-0 loss to the Red Sox on Wednesday. The White Sox have lost all five games against the Red Sox this season by a combined score of 33-4. </p><p>Burke left after 4 ⅓ innings, allowing two runs, five hits and two walks. The Sutton, Massachusetts, native grew up going to Fenway Park and had supporters in attendance.</p><p>“That adds to the frustration,” Burke said. “It’s one of the few times a bunch of my friends and family, people I grew up with, can come watch me. Not to have my best stuff tonight sucks.</p><p>’’From the get-go, the breaking balls weren’t really there. I was really just pitching off my four-seam, two-seam and cutter today, which makes it hard against a lineup like that.’’</p><p>Antonacci made it hard for himself. In the third, he tried to score from second on a grounder to third baseman Caleb Durbin, whose throw pulled Willson Contreras off first base. But Contreras had plenty of time to nab Antonacci at home. </p><p>’’Looking back at it, the whole play was right in front of Contreras,’’ Antonacci said. ’’The amount of years he’s been in the league, that’s an easy play for him. It’s a ball you got to stay put at third on, let Colson [Montgomery] hit us in.’’</p><p>In the seventh, Antonacci misread a fly ball in medium left field and wasn’t in position to make a good throw to get Andruw Monasterio tagging from third.</p><p>’’Tough read on my end,’’ Antonacci said. ’’Had to jump at the very end and wasn’t able to get behind it. I think if I get behind that ball a little bit better, just the way it was hit off the bat, right away I thought it was a broken bat and he kind of flared it into left field. I was coming in right away and just came in a little too hard.’’</p><p>Of course, none of it mattered much because the White Sox couldn't score. Gray allowed three hits and two walks in six innings while striking out eight, getting plenty of swing-and-miss on his sweeper.</p><p>‘‘Sonny Gray had really good stuff tonight, especially to lefties,’’ said White Sox manager Will Venable, who stacked the lineup with five lefties and two switch hitters. ‘‘You saw a lot of spin early [in counts] in the zone that we didn’t fire on. And then later in counts, [we chased] the spin below. He had a lot of different ways he was attacking us, and we just didn’t have any solutions.‘‘</p><p>The White Sox maintained a three-game lead over the Guardians and a four-game lead over the Twins, both of whom lost. At 59-54, the White Sox are the only team in the American League Central above .500.</p><p><b>NOTE:</b> The White Sox designated outfielder <b>Austin Hays</b> for assignment. Hays, who signed a one-year, $6 million deal, had been on a rehab assignment at Triple-A Charlotte for a strained left calf and was hitting well, but White Sox manager <b>Will Venable</b> said he fell entries.title: Sky's DiJonai Carrington finding her form faster than expected in return from injury
entries.summary: <p><b>DiJonai Carrington</b> didn't want to put too much pressure on herself to instantly return to her old form — after all, it had been nearly a year since she'd played in a game.</p><p>Maybe that's partly why her comeback has gone so smoothly.</p><p>In her first three games back, she's averaging 11.7 points off the bench while bringing her usual defensive intensity.</p><p>She’s been pleasantly surprised.</p><p>"I feel like each game I've felt myself getting a little more comfortable trying something new or just being able to take bumps and contact and stay on balance a little bit more," Carrington told the Sun-Times at shootaround Wednesday.</p><p>Carrington waded in with her 3-point shot and pull-up in the first two games, then burst into the paint in her third. She shot a game-high 12 free throws against the Mercury, though she wasn't pleased about missing five of them.</p><p>"Getting to the line don't matter if you don't make them," she said. "So focusing on that as well."</p><p>Carrington wants to be an efficient scorer and keep adding to her game the rest of the season. But overall, she defined success as being able to play without thinking about her injured foot. She said she's been able to do that "in waves," though occasionally she'll catch herself thinking about it on a closeout.</p><p>That particular challenge hasn't slowed her drive to lead, however. She already feels responsible for the team's defensive coverages down the stretch, an area she noted has hurt the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> in clutch games. She thinks being more attentive to body language can help.</p><p>"When [other teams] do go on the runs, I think we show it," Carrington said. "I'm not saying that we don't keep fighting on the court. I think just how we come to the bench, we might overreact, as opposed to just — basketball is a game of runs. They're gonna go on runs. We're gonna go on runs. We have to stay even."</p><p>Overall, returning to the fold has validated for Carrington what her teammates and coaches have been saying all season: This team has fight.</p><p>"We never feel like we're out of the game," she said.</p><p><b>Dual minds</b></p><p>With the Sky and Sparks both entering Wednesday's game holding only an outside shot at the playoffs, each team is approaching the rest of the season with a mix of pragmatism and presence.</p><p>The Sky sat down together after the All-Star break to map out what making the playoffs would require — likely winning 12 or 13 of their final 17 games. But they also want to take it a day at a time, trying to view every matchup as a "one-game season."</p><p>Sparks coach <b>Lynne Roberts</b> is threading the same needle. She said she hasn't done the math on how many games the Sparks need to win — but her players are "not dumb" and know the kind of run they'd need to go on to make up ground.</p><p><b>Stevens returns</b></p><p>Forward <b>Azura Stevens</b> is back with the team after missing four games for personal reasons. Coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> said she'll be ramping up in the coming days. She did not play against the Sparks.</p>

entries.title: Teen killed in North Center e-scooter crash remembered as a 'goofy' boy who was 'always there for everybody'
entries.summary: <p>Alex Blacio was everyone's "rock."</p><p>He was a steady presence in his family, according to his relatives. The teen played volleyball through middle and high school — becoming the captain of the varsity volleyball team at Lake View High School last year, where he was happy to play wherever he was needed — and would often meet up with his middle school friends to play at open gyms.</p><p>Monday, the 16-year-old was riding an e-scooter northbound in the 4100 block of North Western Avenue around 3:35 p.m. when he lost control and was hit by a tractor-trailer, Chicago police said in a statement. He was taken to Illinois Masonic Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>It was his third day at his first job, and though he hadn't been scheduled for work, he was eager to pick up another shift to help out his family, according to his older sister, Andrea Blacio.</p><p>"He showed so much love, he was always there for everybody," she said. "He was such a goofy boy and that's how we'll always remember him."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-680000" name="image-680000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/098dfd5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbb%2F32%2Fcb32ce834736896177f7b6d8cda2%2Fblaciovigil-260806-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/76153a3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbb%2F32%2Fcb32ce834736896177f7b6d8cda2%2Fblaciovigil-260806-7.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/84ebe51/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbb%2F32%2Fcb32ce834736896177f7b6d8cda2%2Fblaciovigil-260806-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Maria Mizhuiri sobs when addressing the dozens of family, friends, and community members attending a vigil for her 16-year-old son Alex Blacio, inside his aunt’s home on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. The number of traffic deaths — which the city had vowed to eliminate by this year — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/08/25/vision-zero-traffic-crash-deaths-pedestrian-cyclist-car-roads-streets" target="_blank" ><u>remains largely where it was 10 years ago</u></a> after a brief pandemic increase.<br></p>

entries.title: Injured White Sox catcher Kyle Teel saves Davis Martin from tipping pitches
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — White Sox catcher Kyle Teel has a skill that came in handy Tuesday night when starting pitcher Davis Martin wasn’t fooling the Red Sox in the first inning.</p><p>“I would say I’m good at picking up patterns, good at pattern recognition,” Teel, who’s on the injured list with a sprained left ankle, told the Sun-Times. “Kind of a big role that I feel like I’ve had on the IL has just been helping our defense, helping our pitchers, trying to protect them as much as possible.”</p><p>While the Red Sox were pounding Martin for six runs and six hits — including back-to-back homers, the first being a grand slam — Teel was watching closely from the dugout, trying to detect whether Martin was tipping pitches.</p><p>“It’s a lot easier from the dugout,” Teel said. “When you’re behind the plate, you’re really focused on catching the ball, trying to frame pitches, throwing guys out, blocking balls. It’s hard to really key in on certain things. But it’s one of those things like, once you see it, you see it.”</p><p>And once Teel saw it, he went to work confirming it.</p><p>“Once I think there’s something, I log it in a notebook and see how many are accurate to what I was putting down,” he said. “If I have a page full of checkmarks, I give it to the coaching staff. They do a really good job, as well, finding tips on guys. It’s a good thing to have as a catcher. It’s something I brought from college, just learning how to do that.”</p><p>It made a difference. After the first, Davis retired 12 of the next 14 batters he faced, inducing mostly soft contact outside of a solo homer in the fifth. But he only lasted two batters into the sixth, departing with 91 pitches, because of that long first inning due to the tipping.</p><p>“Generally, there’s [tipping from] the glove,” Sox pitching coach Zach Bove said, “but guys do different mannerisms, stuff like that, that you would think would never be a thing. For whatever reason, guys create these patterns, and other teams are trying to look at the patterns.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Man loses job after falling ill from cyclosporiasis
entries.summary: <p>It had been years since Edgar Mercado had eaten at a Taco Bell restaurant.</p><p>But early last month, his 14-year-old son wanted some, so he took him to the one near Belmont and Milwaukee avenues.</p><p>“We ate there. A couple of days later, I got sick. My stomach was in pain, like somebody hit me with a hockey stick. I threw up a few times and then the diarrhea. I was dizzy and I couldn’t get out of bed,” said 50-year-old Mercado, who lives in the Jefferson Park neighborhood.</p><p>Once he was able to get to a doctor, Mercado said it was confirmed he had cyclosporiasis, caused by the microscopic parasite cyclospora.</p><p>“I couldn't go to work. I sent them a copy of my situation, and they just let me go,” said Mercado, who had been working for more than a month at a Jewel distribution facility in Melrose Park.</p><p>Mercado plans to sue Taco Bell and Taylor Farms for his illness and loss of wages.</p><p>“We want to make sure that each of our clients are fully and fairly compensated for the losses they've suffered. The second thing we're looking for is to figure out exactly how this happened. How the feces got in the lettuce,” said Ron Simon, Mercado’s attorney, who has not yet filed a lawsuit.</p><p>Simon said his firm represents 300 Illinois residents who claim to have gotten sick from cyclospora.</p><p>“We want to make sure we force Taylor Farms and Taco Bell to take steps to make sure that no one else gets hurt in the future,” Simon said.</p><p>Neither Taco Bell nor Taylor Farms could be reached for comment.</p><p>According to University of Chicago Medicine, cyclospora is a parasite that's very hard to eradicate. Those infected can experience loss of appetite, abdominal cramping and bloating, fatigue, low-grade fever and increased flatulence. Symptoms start two to 14 days after consumption and can last for several weeks.</p><p>“Cyclospora outbreaks are not new. We do see cyclospora outbreaks occur from time to time related to contaminated soil and produce,” Dr. Aniruddha Hazra, associate professor of medicine and director of the infectious disease fellowship program at University of Chicago Medicine, said.</p><p>“I think the concern that many of us have in infectious disease and public health is that the extent at which this outbreak has been allowed to expand is certainly unusual,” Hazra said.</p><p>Hazra said the parasite is very hard to kill. The only way to be safe in eating spinach, for example, is to cook it.</p><p>According to the Illinois Department of Public Health, there have been 995 confirmed or probable cases of cyclospora, with 58 hospitalizations but no deaths, as of Tuesday. In Cook County alone, there have been 112 probable and confirmed cyclosporiasis cases</p><p>Simon, Mercado's attorney, said the federal government could do more.</p><p>“This administration made the decision to cut back on jobs and workers at the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] before the outbreak. As a result, there's not enough people at the CDC to track and keep up with these cases,” Simon said. “They’re working overtime as it is. We just don’t have enough people out there trying to solve the outbreak, and that’s why it’s taking so long.”</p><p>A month after heading to Taco Bell for lunch with his son, Mercado said he’s feeling better. Mercado added he did not take any medication to get well, other than drinking Pedialyte.</p><p>“It’s been about four days now that I’ve been back to normal. It feels good to be back to normal,” Mercado said. “I was praying to God every day to take this away from me.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:mpuente@wbez.org" target="_blank" ><u></u></a><br></p>

You'll keep plugging along at whatever you have to do with your job, your health or a pet. Meanwhile, you'll enjoy little intervals and breaks where you can chat over the fence with someone in a lighthearted way.</p><h2>If today is your birthday</h2><p>Oscar-winning actress Michelle Yeoh (1962) shares your birthday today. entries.title: Former Sky guard Ariel Atkins settles in as everything changes around her
entries.summary: <p>Nothing about Ariel Atkins’ fresh start with the Sparks has gone as planned.</p><p>Not one thing.</p><p>Kelsey Plum, the superstar guard she was supposed to pair with in the backcourt? Traded to the Mercury at the deadline.</p><p>Raegan Pebley, the general manager who took the big bet on Atkins? Fired weeks earlier.</p><p>And the team that talked about championship aspirations during training camp? Dropped to 10th place after losing to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> on Wednesday night.</p><p>Ownership now says they're open to taking a step backward to move forward.</p><p>Atkins understands that uncertainty is part of the business. She also believes everything happens for a reason.</p><p>“It is what it is,” Atkins told the Sun-Times at shootaround Wednesday. “People move. I could not be here next year. I could have been a part of the [Plum] trade. You just never know with sports.</p><p>“Happy to still be here, just where my feet are and locking into who I want to be, not only as a basketball player but as a person. Just staying focused on that. Staying prayed up. Not being upset or angry.”</p><p>Atkins’ transition to the Sparks hasn’t been easy. Her scoring is down, and she is shooting a career-low 30.1% from three.</p><p>But everyone around the Sparks describes Atkins the same way her coaches and teammates did in Chicago: steady, coachable and too valuable defensively to take off the floor, even as she struggled to find her offense.</p><p>That offense began to come when she faced the Sky in late June, finishing with 17 points and six assists. Over the next seven games, Atkins averaged 11.7 points and four assists while shooting 35.1% from three on 5.3 attempts per game — numbers much closer to what she has produced throughout her career.</p><p>“I finally calmed down and started finding my way,” Atkins said.</p><p>Sparks coach Lynne Roberts can see the difference in the way Atkins moves.</p><p>“It’s been fun to see her figure it out,” Roberts said. “You can physically see the burden off her shoulders in terms of trying so hard. Now she’s relaxing and playing in a much more efficient way.”</p><p>Atkins said at the start of the season that she considered re-signing with the Sky. But after a short stint in Chicago that also did not go as planned, she decided she needed a fresh start.</p><p>The Sparks believed her experience and defense could help push them toward contention. Now, nearly every Sparks player has to be wondering: Will this be a long-term home?</p><p>Atkins is the Sparks’ second-highest-paid player, with a $3.41 million deal that runs through 2028. But the person who signed her is gone.</p><p>Farhan Zaidi, special adviser to Sparks owner Mark Walter, recently told the Los Angeles Times that the organization has “to be open for anything” and that “everything has to be on the table.”</p><p>“We pushed in a lot of chips this year, and we had good reason to do that, but the reality is it hasn’t gone as we’d hoped or expected,” Zaidi said.</p><p>While the front office plots its next moves, Atkins is staying in the present. She is learning more about her new teammates — apparently they are Marvel crazy, so they went to see the new Spider-Man together. The day before facing the Sky, the team toured the Obama Presidential Center.</p><p>None of them doubted Atkins would find her footing.</p><p>“It just takes a little time to get your feet wet, chemistry with the girls and everything,” Sparks guard Rae Burrell told the Sun-Times. “We’ve been patient with her and believed in her from the jump.”</p>

entries.title: Dropped charges in reflecting pool 'vandalism' cases show rush to judgment
entries.summary: <p>At a <a class="Link" href="https://www.c-span.org/program/news-conference/us-attorney-jeanine-pirro-announces-charges-related-to-vandalism-of-reflecting-pool/682164" target="_blank" >press conference</a> on July 2, Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, said she had "tremendous evidence" proving that David Hearn had deliberately caused more than $1,000 in damage to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, making him guilty of a <a class="Link" href="https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/22-303" target="_blank" >felony</a> punishable by up to 10 years in prison. That was not true, Pirro admitted Friday, when she <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/31/us/politics/david-hearn-reflecting-pool-vandalism-charges.html" target="_blank" >withdrew</a> the charge against Hearn, a 67-year-old former competitive canoeist.</p><p>Pirro's embarrassing reversal, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/03/politics/jeanine-pirro-removal-reflecting-pool" target="_blank" >enraged</a> President Donald Trump, could be seen as evidence of her <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/08/04/trump-attack-jeanine-pirro-over-reflecting-pool-was-unjustified/" target="_blank" >courage</a> in contradicting her boss's <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/23/us/trump-reflecting-pool-green-peeling.html" target="_blank" >claim</a> that damage to the reflecting pool's newly installed liner was caused by vandals, as opposed to the "rushed and botched installation" she described in her <a class="Link" href="https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/28528042/260731-hearn.pdf" target="_blank" >motion</a> to dismiss the indictment against Hearn. But it also raises questions about Pirro's decision to charge Hearn given what she knew at the time, which suggests she was keen to make an example of him even though there was already reason to doubt his guilt.</p><p>By the time Pirro obtained the <a class="Link" href="https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/david-hearn-olympian-lincoln-reflecting-pool-indictment.pdf" target="_blank" >indictment</a>, news outlets had <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/23/us/trump-reflecting-pool-green-peeling.html" target="_blank" >reported</a> that <a class="Link" href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/lincoln-memorial-reflecting-pool-liner-appears-falling-apart/story?id=134002251" target="_blank" >parts</a> of the reflecting pool's blue liner, which was installed under an unusual <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/08/us/politics/reflecting-pool-trump-contract.html" target="_blank" >no-bid contract</a> by a company that had never done work for the federal government before, were <a class="Link" href="https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/the-paint-is-already-peeling-in-trumps-renovated-washington-reflecting-pool-4750917" target="_blank" >coming loose</a>. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/white-house/4614945/lincoln-reflecting-pool-blue-paint-peeling-algae/" target="_blank" >earliest reports</a> appeared on <a class="Link" href="https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/the-paint-is-already-peeling-in-trumps-renovated-washington-reflecting-pool-4750917" target="_blank" >June 18</a>, the day before Hearn was <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/06/20/cyclist-arrested-reflecting-pool-denies-trump-vandalism-claims/" target="_blank" >arrested</a> and two weeks before his indictment.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4f0000" name="module-4f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>By Hearn's account, he paused during a bike ride and reached into the pool to touch a floating piece of liner because he was curious about what it felt like.</p><p>"I didn't vandalize anything," he <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/06/20/cyclist-arrested-reflecting-pool-denies-trump-vandalism-claims/" target="_blank" >told</a> The Washington Post. "I didn't destroy or break or peel anything."</p><p>Interior Department employees told a different story. The initial U.S. Park Police report, which Pirro quotes in her motion, said Hearn saw "a big piece of material flapping in the water and began to grab at it," citing "a witness" who said Hearn "began to rip and pull at a chunk of liner material."</p><p>Two National Park Service employees said Hearn was yanking at the flap and "further damaging this compromised area." In other words, everyone conceded that the liner was already coming loose, and the only dispute concerned whether and to what extent Hearn had "maliciously" compounded the damage.</p><p>At her news conference the day of the indictment, Pirro embraced the Interior Department's account, saying park service employees "observed Hearn actually forcefully and violently pulling up and removing the bottom liner with both hands."</p><p>Now, she says she was too quick to believe that story, blaming the Interior Department for concealing relevant information about recognized problems with the liner installation.</p><p>According to the information provided by the Interior Department, Pirro says, "The damage was entirely caused by vandals." But judging from internal documents that her office subsequently obtained, the damage "was the result of flawed installation by the contractor."</p><p>While those documents may have illuminated the extent of the problem, it should not have been news to Pirro, since it had been discussed in news reports (including stories based on Interior Department <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/23/us/trump-reflecting-pool-green-peeling.html" target="_blank" >records</a>) weeks before she stood in front of a podium and accused Hearn of a felony. But Pirro disregarded that alternative explanation, apparently because she was eager to punish "unchecked vandalism" of "our sacred monuments," which she said was "a priority not only for the president, but for myself as well."</p><p>That priority overrode the question of whether Hearn was provably guilty of vandalism, which should have been the only consideration in the decision to charge him.</p><p>"The government's approach was ready, fire, aim," Hearn's lawyers <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/31/us/politics/david-hearn-reflecting-pool-vandalism-charges.html" target="_blank" >said</a>. Something similar seems to have happened with three other cases against alleged reflecting pool vandals, which Pirro's office also <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/03/us/reflecting-pool-charges.html" target="_blank" >dropped</a>.</p><p>"I disagree 100% with Jeanine Pirro," Trump <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117021210137447022" target="_blank" >said</a> Saturday. "I guess she choked," he <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/03/politics/jeanine-pirro-removal-reflecting-pool" target="_blank" >added</a> Monday, saying he was "really disappointed" in her because "she folded like an umbrella." </p><p>For the president, the question of individual guilt or innocence remains irrelevant.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-960000" name="module-960000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Woman Has No Clue Why Friend Group Ousted Her
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Four years ago, my cousin "Roy" introduced me to his friends, who, once a month, have a party at the home of one of the couples. We would eat and then play a form of dominoes. It was raucous and fun. The second time I went, a couple in the group told me that now I was "part of the family." I always had fun and laughed a lot, which I hadn't experienced much after my husband died years ago. Roy even invited me to go on a couple of cruises with six people from the group.</p><p>At the end of the last cruise, everyone shunned me, except for Roy, who instead was cruel and insulting to me. Abby, no one will tell me what horrible thing I could've said or done to make everyone so furious. I told Roy that he knew I'd never do anything to deliberately hurt or offend someone I loved. He never explained anything to me, and although I reached out to five members of the group, they won't answer me either.</p><p>How can I apologize if I don't know what I said or did wrong? Roy has since died, so I can't pursue the matter with him, and I'm wondering if I should try again with any of them to find out why they ghosted me? — <i>LONELY WITHOUT THEM IN MISSOURI</i></p><p><b>DEAR LONELY:</b> If the reason you want to keep pursuing this after four years is to reestablish social relationships with these people, I think the ship has sailed on that score. If, for your own peace of mind, you would like an answer, consider approaching your cousin Roy's friends one last time and asking about it. Whatever the answer may be, however, it is important that you enlarge your social circle and move forward. Continuing to dwell on this hurt will not be helpful at this point.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Six months ago, my wife and I hired a cleaning company to help around the house once a month. It has been a big help because my wife has arthritis. Even though her arthritis is debilitating at times, she insists on still working at least part time.</p><p>When "Helen," the woman who cleans our home, arrives, we offer her tea or something before she starts to clean. Recently, she asked my wife if she worked, and my wife responded that she works part time as a librarian. Helen's response was, "Oh, I wish I could work part time."</p><p>My wife is 64 and worked full time until two years ago. Helen is probably in her 30s. I didn't appreciate Helen's demeanor. Her response had a hint of jealousy. My wife and I are quiet people. We dislike strife. How can we politely tell Helen she talks too much? We don't mind for a little while, but she talks almost the entire time she's at our home. — <i>UNRECEPTIVE AUDIENCE IN NEW YORK</i></p><p><b>DEAR U.A.:</b> A way to accomplish that would be to stop offering Helen "tea or something" when she arrives, which should give her less time to socialize. Another would be to make it a habit not to be in the same room with her while she's working. I'm sure you and your wife can find something else to do while the place is being cleaned. You could even go out for coffee or lunch unless your intuition is telling you she can't be trusted. If that's the case, you need another cleaning person.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: Inside the nearly five-month labor lockout at BP's Whiting refinery
entries.summary: <p><i>This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WBEZ and </i><a class="Link" href="http://grist.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Grist</i></a><i>, a nonprofit environmental media organization.</i></p><p>Jessica Skalka, 37, rounded the corner of a homemade bar in her dad’s garage, passing a framed collage of cutout newspaper clips marking the end of the 99-day strike at BP’s Whiting, Indiana, refinery in 2015. A row of championship banners for the Chicago Cubs, Bears and White Sox hung high across one wall, while a light-up “Donnie’s Man Cave” sign glowed nearby.</p><p>She picked up an empty blue-and-orange Bears-themed bucket from the counter, shook it, and asked, “No candy today?”</p><p>“Yeah, well, I’m not working right now,” said Donald Skalka, 62, from across the garage.</p><p>Until mid-March, father and daughter worked at BP’s sprawling plant in Whiting, Indiana, the largest inland oil refinery in North America.</p><p>There, Donald had spent nearly two decades working his way up to a job in the control room, where he monitored the refinery’s operations from behind a bank of screens. The plant processed approximately 440,000 barrels of crude oil every day, and Donald kept the electricity and steam-generating machinery at the plant running. Donald’s son worked there, too, as did Jessica. Donald met his longtime girlfriend, Renee Pleitner, during his onboarding at the plant. She’s a third-generation refinery worker.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-250000" Now, longtime refinery workers worry Big Oil is experimenting with a new playbook to break union power, undermine national collective bargaining, and remake its workforce.</p><p>BP began negotiating with the union in early January ahead of the previous contract’s expiration at the end of that month. But two months into discussions, after 98 percent of USW Local 7-1 members voted to reject what the fossil fuel company called its last, best, and final offer, the company issued a lockout order. The proposal would have held up wages, cut jobs, and expanded the use of artificial intelligence, according to the union.</p><p>In an emailed statement to WBEZ, BP objected to the union’s Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The lockout also “allowed for a safe and orderly transition of operations,” Cesar said. The union’s 24-hour notice requirement to strike and disrupt refinery operations “presented safety and operational risk,” BP wrote in an earlier statement, and necessitated a continuity plan.</p><p>For Skalka, the March email notifying him that he wouldn’t be returning to work until further notice was gutting.</p><p>“The gamut of emotions when I had to face my family, it was a lot,” he said.</p><p>Born and raised in the northwest corner of Indiana, most of Skalka’s family had worked at industrial facilities. His father worked at cement factories and later built parts for the nearby steel mills. An uncle was a shipbuilder on the East Side of Chicago.</p><p>Skalka was eventually entrusted with an important role at the refinery. From the control room, he was responsible for identifying broken pumps, mechanical hiccups, and mystery leaks.</p><p>“There's a little bit of danger to it,” he said. “When you swipe in with your time card, you have to bring your A game.”</p><p>All the same, he loved the job — and his daughter noticed.</p><p>It was an exciting, breakneck-paced lifestyle, and the pay was good. She peppered her dad with questions, took a qualifying test, passed, and eventually earned a spot. Donald Skalka Jr., Skalka’s son, spent approximately a decade working at a nearby steel mill. When an opportunity at the refinery came up a year and a half ago, he took it. It was a decision his father encouraged.</p><p>“He's one of the 800 like the rest of us, and he's going, ‘Dad, I don't know if I should’ve listened to you.’ Well, I didn't know at the time that was going to happen,” Skalka said. “At the time, on paper, everything seemed better; you're trying to have a better quality of life.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>United Steelworkers Local 7-1 member Jessica Skalka is one of 800 BP workers locked out of their jobs.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The lockout has reshaped his home life in other ways too. Jessica found temporary work. Her brother returned to a job at the mill. Donald and Renee are holding out, living on a budget that keeps shrinking. They’ve swapped cable for streaming and are using rabbit-ear antennas for free local channels. They also paid their utility bills months in advance to avoid a power shutoff in the future.</p><p>“You get rid of the non-essentials right away,” Skalka said. “The thermostat stays higher, there's less in the grocery cart, you don't eat out obviously hardly at all anymore.”</p><p>They pass the time filling poster boards with pictures of good times on the picket line. And they aren’t done picketing. Skalka pilots the union’s second-hand minibus, a stout, cream-colored vehicle, shuttling picketing union members between four different entrances. Union members have been assigned shifts to protest — four shifts a day, four protesters a shift. The schedule has allowed workers to find other employment and extend their ability to hold out during the lockout.</p><p>Donald goes on his off days too, when Pleitner is on the schedule, and she does the same for him. “We just kind of make it a family event,” Skalka said.</p><p>By now, he’s used to the new routine. What he’s still wrapping his head around is a new, more aggressive tack from his employer — one that has pushed his family, friends, and coworkers to their limits.</p><p>“This time it seems they're in a union-breaking mode,” he said, “They’re following a playbook.”</p><h2>The origin story</h2><p>Union leaders trace the origins of BP’s strategy to Texas. In 2021, Exxon, the nation’s largest oil and gas company, locked out approximately 650 unionized workers from its Beaumont, Texas, refinery when they rejected a “last, best, and final offer,” which would have frozen wages and ended some union seniority rights. At the time, the Beaumont workers were already operating outside the framework of the National Oil Bargaining Program, an effort dating back to the 1960s to negotiate industry-wide standards for wages, health care, and workplace safety.</p><p>The program exerts leverage by aligning approximately 200 refinery bargaining units around the same contract timelines, preventing unions from being pitted against each other, and establishing a national standard. Without that collective leverage, the Beaumont refinery workers were at a disadvantage. The Texas lockout lasted 10 months and ended in March 2022. When workers returned to their jobs, they did so under a weaker contract that gave ExxonMobil authority over job assignments, stripping the union of its previous role in determining a quarter of them.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c90000" name="image-c90000"></a> <picture negotiations, Jordan Marcks, as a director of employees and labor relations, while that lockout was ongoing. Schultz sees similarities between BP’s proposal and Exxon’s plan for the Texas refinery. For one, BP is pushing a contract term that would put the Whiting refinery out of step with the National Oil Bargaining Program. It is also looking to eliminate jobs and union oversight.</p><p>“They obviously liked that playbook,” he said. “They're trying to bring that flavor up here to Northwest Indiana,” Schultz added.</p><p>When reached for comment about Marcks’ employment history and alleged tactics, a BP spokesperson said the company “does not comment on personnel matters.” Marcks did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Mike Smith, the chair of the National Oil Bargaining for the United Steelworkers, said it’s not totally clear yet whether the lockouts reflect a new tactic for Big Oil. “Whether this is an individual's idea who happens to have been involved in both of those lockouts, or if this is a strategy — that's still to be determined,” he said.</p><h2>“A good fight on their hands”</h2><p>With the workers locked out, the squat union hall has transformed into an all-hours crisis center. Makeshift shelves in a corner carry everything from simple groceries like canned food and pasta to diapers and baby formula. The formula and diapers are typically the first to go, according to Michelle O'Shaughnessy, a union member who has been helping run the improvised pantry since the lockout started.</p><p>The local community has also rallied behind the refinery workers. “We have some faithful restaurants who are very good to us,” O'Shaughnessy said. The union has a strike fund that helps pay some bills, but members do not receive cash payments or salaries. Other organizations have also stepped up to assist with mortgage payments and help apply for SNAP benefits.</p><p>While the fight plays out, Skalka is hunkering down, preparing for a long road back to work. He’s not sure when or if he’ll get to put his BP uniform on again. What he does know is that he, his family, his nearly 800 USW brothers and sisters, and the rest of Northwest Indiana are determined to win.</p><p>“We're still going to keep living our lives; it's not gonna deter the hardworking people in Northwest Indiana,” Skalka said. "They've got a good fight on their hands, and we're gonna give it to them.”</p>

entries.title: Court Theatre series takes audiences on a tour through 100 years of Black theater
entries.summary: <p>When Ron “OJ” Parson thinks about the past century of Black arts, he can’t help but zero in on one genre: theater.</p><p>The resident artist of the University of Chicago’s Court Theatre, Parson had an idea about a decade ago alongside his friend, the Chicago-based director Chuck Smith.</p><p>Both Parson and Smith have a reputation for being former collaborators of the legendary playwright August Wilson.</p><p>Parson is on the cusp of directing all 10 plays of Wilson’s famed “American Century Cycle,” a set of 10 ambitious works that dramatize the lives of Black Americans in different decades, with a 2027 production of “Joe Turner’s Come and Gone.”</p><p>“Chuck Smith said he was going to do an August Wilson reading series,” said Parson. “I thought we should do something like that at Court, but from a different angle. We'll do the Black Theater movement.”</p><p>That idea led to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.courttheatre.org/season-tickets/spotlight-reading-series/theodoreward/" target="_blank" >Spotlight Series,</a> which has highlighted Black playwrights both historic and contemporary in its decade of existence. Parson, who studied theater at the University of Michigan in the 1970s, wanted to familiarize up-and-coming artists and current audiences with classic Black plays. In the early days, the series featured the work of artists like Ed Bullins (“The Taking of Miss Janie”) and Joseph A. Walker (“The River Niger”).</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ef0000" name="module-ef0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><a class="Link" href="https://www.courttheatre.org/season-tickets/spotlight-reading-series/theodoreward/" target="_blank" ><b>Spotlight Series</b></a><br><br><b>When:</b> Through Aug. 22; highlights include Kuumba Theatre Archive Unfurling on Aug. 9 and “A Womanist Trilogy: Hurston, Richards, and Kennedy” on Aug. 13<br><br><b>Where:</b> Court Theatre, Harold Washington Library Center, University of Chicago Campus<br><br><b>Info:</b> Programs are free with registration. Sold out events have wait lists available.</div> </div><p>In 2016, they did a reading of “The River Niger” at a park in Englewood.</p><p>“That's how it started, but it ended up also including Latino plays, Native American plays, and plays from different cultures,” Parson said.</p><p>Parson also wanted to share the experience of theater with communities that may not have access to shows. In 2018, when the pair did a reading of Native playwright William S. Yellow Robe’s “The Independence of Eddie Rose,” they held it at the American Indian Center.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A.C. Smith (left) and Kylah Renee Jones perform in the Goodman Theatre’s production of August Wilson’s “Joe Turner’s Come and Gone” in 2024. Two Chicago directors with mutual admiration for Wilson joined forces to create the Spotlight Series a decade ago. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by Liz Lauren</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“It was a combination of introducing new artists, but also marketing for the theater,” said Parson. “I was trying to introduce the theater to other neighborhoods in the city, so that the people would say, ‘Oh, they're doing something different. Let's buy a ticket.’ Because we would then offer them discounts.”</p><p>A decade ago, Parson, along with Court’s former community programs manager Aaron Mays, got the Spotlight Series up, running and into neighborhoods. But after the pandemic, Court’s director of engagement, Kamilah Rashied, ushered the program into a new generation.</p><p>“I don't want to say ‘revamp’,” Rashied said of the series. “I think it was reconsidering the program to make it all it could be with the resources we have.”</p><p>For the 10-year anniversary, Rashied envisions a celebration of 100 years of Black theater. She wants to connect past-to-present — but not in a linear way. She wants the years to meld together for a timeless experience that honors and presents the work of playwrights and theater companies from the past, while also spinning the art form forward with contemporary actors and theater companies also being highlighted.</p><p>“When I was thinking about what we were going to do to celebrate that 10 years of Spotlight, I really was like, ‘How do we do that’? There's so many writers. There's so many levels there,” she said. “And it just came to me: A century of Black progress. And that was tied to my awareness that the 100th anniversary of Black History Month, which had been Negro History Week, had just turned 100.”</p><p>Inspired by the idea of connecting the historical to the contemporary, she went to work crafting a series that bridged generations of theater.</p><p>One reading, on Aug. 14, will highlight a new company on the South Side: Definition Theatre, located adjacent to the University of Chicago campus in Hyde Park. Definition and Court are neighbors. The new company, co-founded by millennial artistic director Tyrone Phillips, is known for staging new works by and for underrepresented communities and artists of color.</p><p>The Spotlight Series will stage a reading of “Are you ready to smash white things?” by Definition ensemble member Ireon Roach.</p><p>Looking to the past, the series will feature an event at Harold Washington Library Center that invites audiences to participate in a cultural “unfurling” of Kuumba Theatre. Founded in 1969, Kuumba was once a prominent South Side theater. The event pairs the library’s archival collection with conversations with former ensemble members and invites the public to also share memories of the former playhouse.</p><p>“This is an informal way of learning,” she said of the event. “This is also remembering as a community. This is also consciousness raising. It's like, ‘Wait, did you know that these thriving Black spaces were here on the South Side’? Let's resurface that information for your awareness.”</p><p>Keeping with the theme of connecting old and new, Parson will do a reading of August Wilson's one-man “How I Learned What I Learned.” And for him, this is a reunion many years in the making. Parson was in Seattle when the famed playwright performed the play himself, but he was directing a show in the suburbs and missed Wilson’s performance after getting lost on the bus.</p><p>“I’ve regretted that for all these years,” he said. “Now I get to direct it — and be in it.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2025/11/07/we-see-you-white-american-theatre-diversity-equity-inclusion-arts-chicago-dei" >Did the ‘We See You, White American Theater’ movement spark change in Chicago?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2024/11/26/black-ensemble-theater-building-cultural-village-uptown-expansion-artist-residences-retail-studio" >Black Ensemble Theater steps closer to creating ‘cultural village’ with Uptown expansion</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/5/18/23112624/court-theatre-regional-tony-award-2022-broadway-charles-newell-hyde-park-university-of-chicago" >Court Theatre to receive 2022 Regional Theatre Tony Award</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: No laughing matter: Survey finds nearly 16% of Chicago comedians lack access to health insurance
entries.summary: <p>As the Health Alliance for Chicago Comedians launched, Elizabeth Grossman started to hear from other artists — like musicians and actors — seeking solutions for accessing health care.</p><p>This week, the Chicago-based group released its first <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagohacc.org/research" target="_blank" >report</a> detailing their survey of 110 comedians who either lived in Chicago or performed in the city during the first half of this year. Of those surveyed, nearly 16% are uninsured.</p><p>Another 24% buy their insurance through Get Covered Illinois, the state’s Affordable Care Act market exchange, according to the report. Another 8% depend on Medicaid, a federal health program for low-income individuals.</p><p>For Grossman, the survey results highlight how comedians are among those at risk of losing access to affordable health care due to changes on the federal level to the ACA and Medicaid. Last year, Congress allowed COVID-era enhanced <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/12/18/obamacare-aca-tax-credits-expiring-premiums-congress-january-spike-health-care-insurance" target="_blank" >tax credits</a> to expire. Those subsidies had made buying health insurance through the ACA more affordable.</p><p>The percentage of uninsured Chicago comedians is higher than the national rate for people age 64 and under. Of that group, about 10% lack health insurance, according to KFF, which conducts health policy research and polling.</p><p>“I think it’s a really good microcosm of the rest of the world,” Grossman, who co-founded the alliance, said about the survey results. “They’re artists but they run the gamut in terms of other jobs that they have, or income levels, or background.”</p><p>Nearly 35% of comedians indicated they get insurance through their employer, and another 16% access it through a parent or spouse, the survey found.</p><p>Other sectors of the arts also are seeing the need for more help in getting health coverage, especially since the COVID pandemic, said Michael Anderson, the managing advisor for the Chicago Dance Health Fund. The fund provides grants to dancers for health and wellness as well as for those undergoing critical medical care, such as cancer treatments.</p><p>“As health care becomes more and more expensive, I think a lot of artists, especially dancers I’ll speak for more specifically, who are usually younger … they’re under-insured or they have very high premiums,” Anderson said. “They have very expensive plans. So the need for something like the Chicago Dance Health Fund or some of these other organizations are just paramount for artists that are working today.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-aa0000" name="html-embed-module-aa0000"></a><div style="min-height:434px" id="datawrapper-vis-eHvau"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/eHvau/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-eHvau"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/eHvau/full.png" alt="How do Chicago comedians get health insurance? (Donut Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The Health Alliance for Chicago Comedians aims to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/27/chicago-comedians-could-get-help-buying-health-insurance-from-new-fundraising-alliance" target="_blank" >launch a pilot program</a> later this year that would subsidize the cost of health insurance through Get Covered Illinois for about 10 local stand-up comics. So far, they’ve raised $20,000 toward that program, Grossman said. They would like to raise closer to $60,000, and they also anticipate tracking data on the pilot’s participants.</p><p>“Our hypothesis is that providing this little bit of cushion for them is really going to help, that this is something that is holding them back that either they’re not touring or they’re not making as much money as they want to do,” Grossman said. “That we are going to see people really thrive.”</p><p>In the survey, some comedians indicated they didn’t participate in tours because they couldn’t afford to or were worried about getting sick without insurance on the road, Grossman said.</p><p>Some of the comedians they have been surveying are tied to the Lincoln Lodge, a nonprofit independent comedy venue in Logan Square. The Lincoln Lodge is exploring joining a group health insurance program through the Greater Ravenswood Chamber of Commerce, said Kelsie Huff, director of marketing and training center program development for the venue.</p><p>They are looking into whether comedians who perform at the Lincoln Lodge also could join the plan as a way to get health insurance, Huff said, adding that comedians, like other artists, aren’t paid well because society doesn’t value art.</p><p>“The average comedian, just like the average artist — just like, I dare to say, the average American — is being devastated by the health care insurance,” Huff said.</p>

entries.title: 30 months in prison for man who fired gun near immigration agents during Operation Midway Blitz
entries.summary: <p>A federal judge sentenced a man to 30 months in prison after he admitted he fired a gun “in proximity of” U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents during the final days of Operation Midway Blitz last fall.</p><p>In sentencing Hector Gomez on Thursday, U.S. District Judge Matthew Kennelly said his actions could have led to a far more tragic outcome.</p><p>Kennelly stressed the seriousness of Gomez's actions on Nov. 8, saying that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/27/midway-blitz-ice-border-patrol-little-village-trump-bovino" target="_blank" >firing a gun</a> during a "potentially volatile situation" could have put both protesters and federal agents agents at risk. “It's great that it didn't happen, but it's just a really bad situation,” Kennelly said.</p><p>For those reasons, Kennelly sentenced Gomez to 30 months in prison, with a year of supervised release — though Gomez likely will be deported to Mexico after he's released from prison. </p><p>Gomez's sentencing is the first in a nonimmigration criminal case stemming from the Trump administration's deportation campaign in the Chicago area last year. Gomez pleaded guilty in April to illegally possessing a firearm as a felon.</p><p>Federal prosecutors have charged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >33 known defendants</a> with nonimmigration crimes tied to Midway Blitz. Twenty-four were cleared; five others are on track to see their charges dismissed. Charges against two individuals were still pending.</p><p>Gomez's attorney, Michael Monaco, asked the judge to impose an 18-month sentence, saying Gomez regretted his actions and that his judgment had been impaired by alcohol.</p><p>Monaco said the shooting happened during one of several "binge-drinking" episodes for Gomez, 46, who began drinking at age 14. According to his lawyers, Gomez was drinking the night before and resumed drinking as soon as he woke up the morning of the incident.</p><p>Assistant U.S. Attorney Jill Bhalakia said Gomez was driving under the influence when he fired at least two shots near Border Patrol agents in the 2400 block of South Kedzie Avenue.</p><p>Prosecutors said Gomez fled the scene before parking near the 3100 block of West 26th Street. Around 2:30 p.m., Gomez got out of the Jeep, brandished the gun in front of an unidentified person and "laughed profusely" while doing so.</p><p>Chicago police later found Gomez sitting in the driver's seat with the gun in his lap and beer bottles in the center console, according to prosecutors.</p><p>Bhalakia said Gomez has been removed from the United States multiple times, was convicted of illegal entry in 2010 and became the subject of a final order of removal on Dec. 10. She noted he was also convicted last year of aggravated unlawful possession of a weapon.</p><p>Though Kennelly acknowledged Gomez had a drinking problem, he said there was no guarantee he wouldn’t “find himself in these kinds of situations again.”</p><p>Kennelly said he found the recommended 30-month sentence surprisingly low given the seriousness of Gomez’s conduct, but said he would respect the prosecutors’ recommendation and wouldn't increase the sentence.</p><p>Gomez addressed Kennelly during the sentencing hearing, saying he was “ashamed” and “regretful” of his actions. He said his time in prison had given him an opportunity to reflect on the situation and “ I am now a better person.”</p><p>Gomez said when he returns to Mexico he will reunite with his wife and their three children.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/27/midway-blitz-ice-border-patrol-little-village-trump-bovino" target="_blank" >Man admits opening fire near border agents during Operation Midway Blitz</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/13/midway-blitz-hector-gomez-bovino-trump-little-village" target="_blank" >In first Midway Blitz sentencing, feds want 30-month prison term for man who fired gun near immigration agents</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >Tracking every known federal prosecution in Chicago tied to Trump’s deportation blitz</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Prosecutors: Darien home invasion suspect flees with cellphone, sparking high-speed police chase, standoff
entries.summary: <p>A DuPage County judge Thursday ordered a man held in custody after he allegedly broke into a Darien home and fled with the injured homeowner's cellphone, sparking a high-speed police chase and a standoff that ended with his arrest in the village of Homer Glen earlier this week. </p><p>Michael Joseph Lahey, 32, appeared before DuPage County Judge Joshua Dieden, who denied pre-trial release for Lahey, who was charged with two counts of home invasion, aggravated fleeing and eluding and misdemeanor theft, according to a statement from the DuPage County state’s attorney’s office.</p><p>Lahey, of the 13000 block of Maverick Trail in the village of Homer Glen, is due back in court on Aug. 31, according to the statement.</p><p>The situation unfolded about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/04/homer-glen-neighborhood-ordered-to-shelter-in-place-due-to-barricaded-situation" target="_blank" >2:20 p.m. Tuesday in the 1400 block of Sequoia Drive </a>when a Darien homeowner called police after hearing the sound of breaking-glass and found Lahey standing outside of his home, according to the statement.</p><p>Lahey then allegedly hurled a hunk of broken glass at the homeowner, causing a “significant” laceration to the man's arm and a cut on his torso, the statement said. Lahey — who had burst into the home through the smashed out front window — also threw a stool at the victim before speeding away in a Ford Bronco SUV with the homeowner’s cellphone, according to the statement.</p><p>The homeowner — who escaped by running out the back door — was taken to a local hospital for a laceration to his left upper arm, a puncture wound to his left torso and bruising to his stomach.</p><p>Responding Darien police officers spotted Lahey fleeing in the SUV, sparking a high-speed, 11 mile-long pursuit of Lahey, who jumped a curb and plowed through a parking lot, reaching speeds in excess of 75 miles per hour in a 35 mile per hour zone, according to the statement.</p><p>Additionally, Lahey sped through a construction zone while workers were on duty and drove into oncoming traffic on multiple occasions, according to the statement. </p><p>Officers terminated the chase out of safety concerns after entering Will County but a short while later, Lahey holed himself up at his own home in the 13,000 block of Maverick Trail, according to Darien Police Deputy Chief Austin Jump. </p><p>Will County sheriff’s deputies responded there around 4 p.m. to help other police with a “barricaded subject,” the office said on social media. </p><p>About 7 p.m. officers obtained a search warrant for his home, and began hours-long negotiations to try and have the situation end peacefully, Jump said. </p><p>But Lahey would not willingly come out of his home and DuPage and Will County SWAT teams breached the single-family home, and arrested Lahey at 11:20 p.m., Jump said.</p><p>Lahey, who was the only person inside the house, declined medical attention and a shelter-in-place for the area was lifted about 11 p.m., officials said. </p><p>When asked what could possibly have been Lahey’s motive, Jump indicated it was “not just” the property crime of the stolen cellphone but declined to elaborate.</p><p>“The type of aggressive, unpredictable and violent behavior that shattered an innocent man’s sense of safety and security in his own home and sent him to the hospital with serious injuries, as alleged in this case, has no place in civilized society and will not be tolerated in DuPage County,” DuPage County State’s Attorney Robert Berlins said in the statement.</p><p>“The victim in this case has a long road to recovery ahead of him and I wish him well as he recovers both physically and emotionally,” said Berlin in the statement.<br></p>
