entries.title: Expanding Bears RB D'Andre Swift's role all about creating overwhelming set of options for coach Ben Johnson
entries.summary: <p>Last season was arguably the best <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> running back D’Andre Swift has run in his career, though he doesn’t believe it’s the best he’ll ever run.</p><p>For as good of a career as he’s already had with the Bears, Eagles and Lions, he’s still just 27 and might not have peaked yet. The Bears have few weapons as capable of converting a seemingly simple play into a huge gain, and Swift has the potential to be the engine of their offense as a do-it-all back.</p><p>“There’s a lot more out there for me,” he said.</p><p>Good, because Bears coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> was thinking the same thing.</p><p>Swift took a major step last season by showing he can be a reliable north-south runner between the tackles in his reunion with Johnson, who was on staff with the Lions when they drafted him and traded him away. His numbers jumped across the board, especially a spike from 3.8 to 4.9 yards per carry, and he ran for a career-high 1,087 yards and nine touchdowns.</p><p>He was a big factor in the team going from 25th in rushing in 2024 to third last season. There was more to it than him, of course, as the Bears overhauled their offensive line, drafted a solid No. 2 running back in Kyle Monangai, installed a smarter offense under Johnson and hired an incredibly overqualified running backs coach in Eric Bieniemy.</p><p>But there still was some untapped potential.</p><p>The first area Swift pointed to was explosive runs, defined as 20-plus yards, and he was 17th in the NFL with five. Some quarterbacks had that many.</p><p>Johnson thinks big anyway, so he embraces that ambition. In his mind, every play he calls could be a touchdown.</p><p>The balance for Swift, however, is to find those explosives without losing sight of how important it is to steadily plow forward. The side-to-side running hurt him in 2024, and Bieniemy established a guiding principle of “get 4 1/2 yards” first, then get greedy.</p><p>Bieniemy went back to the Chiefs as offensive coordinator in the offseason, and the Bears running backs don’t use that motto anymore under new coach Eric Studesville. It must remain ingrained in their mindset, though, and Studesville has more than two decades experience coaching NFL backs and worked on staff with Johnson under coach Adam Gase with the Dolphins, so he likely has his own way of implementing that approach.</p><p>“That's something that will stick with me for sure,” Swift assured.</p><p>Can he do both? Swift credited himself for doing “a good job of putting the ball where I was supposed to, for the most part” last season, and wants to keep doing so. The big-play hunting starts when he gets to the second or third level of the defense, the territory in which “it’s my job to take it the rest of the way.”</p><p>Johnson and Swift both mentioned the passing attack as the other aspect of the offense where Swift can make more impact.</p><p>He had a career-low 34 catches last season, totaling 299 yards and a touchdown, but three of those receptions went for 25 or more yards. While Swift doesn’t get as much attention as wide receivers Rome Odunze and Luther Burden and tight end Colston Loveland, he’s probably the most low-risk, high-reward option quarterback Caleb Williams has.</p><p>The play that lingers in everyone’s minds, especially Johnson’s, was in the Week 6 victory over the Commanders on Monday Night Football. Williams threw to Swift just past the line of scrimmage with no one near him. Swift slipped two defenders on his way to a 55-yard touchdown.</p><p>ESPN broadcaster and Hall of Famer Troy Aikman called it “just luck,” which riled up Johnson and Williams and simply wasn’t true. There’s nothing lucky about the Bears getting the ball to Swift in space. It’s savvy.</p><p>Johnson has known that for a long time, and Swift got 148 targets over the 2021 and ’22 seasons with the Lions when Johnson was passing-game coordinator and offensive coordinator.</p><p>He said this week he loves where Swift is at as a runner and he wants to “continue to look at and challenge him on” opportunities as a receiver.</p><p>That idea is partly Johnson’s seemingly limitless creativity, but also setting up the offense for contingencies. Having plenty of backup plans was a hallmark of his first season as head coach.</p><p>Do the Bears really need Swift to do more damage as a receiver when they have Odunze, Burden, Loveland, Cole Kmet, Khalif Raymond and rookie speedster Zavion Thomas? Probably not. But that list of options could be cut in half any given week because of injuries or an opponent stacked with elite defenders who can negate them.</p><p>It’s all about coming to the line of scrimmage with as many pieces and as much versatility as possible. Then the offense becomes overwhelming.<br></p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Lo que debes saber sobre la ciclosporiasis, infección que está provocando diarrea en Illinois
entries.summary: <p>En Illinois se han confirmado 995 casos de la enfermedad que causa diarrea, ciclosporiasis, confirmó el martes el Departamento de Salud Pública del estado.</p><p>La ciclosporiasis no se considera mortal y es en casos raros, una molestia que puede presentar complicaciones, aseguró la Dra. Emily Landon, especialista en enfermedades infecciosas de University of Chicago Medicine. En Illinois, 58 personas han sido hospitalizadas, según el Departamento de Salud Pública de Illinois (IDPH).</p><p>La mayoría de las personas en Illinois que contrajeron la enfermedad habían viajado recientemente: 193 personas internacionalmente y 631 domésticamente. No está claro si las otras 171 personas viajaron.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e30000" name="module-e30000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Por lo general, se reportan más casos de ciclosporiasis en verano, pero este año se ha observado un número especialmente alto, dijeron funcionarios de salud.</p><p>El aumento en Illinois forma parte de una mayor cantidad de casos en varios estados. En Michigan, que ha estado en el centro de un brote a nivel nacional, dos personas con condiciones de salud significativas murieron, según anunciaron las autoridades sanitarias el 3 de agosto, quienes señalaron que la ciclosporiasis y la deshidratación contribuyeron a las muertes.</p><p>Hasta el miércoles, el Departamento de Salud y Servicios Humanos de Michigan informó de <a class="Link" href="https://www.michigan.gov/mdhhs/keep-mi-healthy/infectious-diseases/infectious-disease-outbreaks" target="_blank" >12,218 casos</a>. En todo el país, los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades (CDC) reportaron 1,947 casos en nueve estados, cifra muy inferior a la de Michigan por sí solo. Esos casos estuvieron vinculados a comer en Taco Bell, según los CDC y la Administración de Alimentos y Medicamentos (FDA).</p><p>Esto es lo que debes saber sobre la ciclosporiasis en Illinois.</p><h3>¿Qué es la ciclosporiasis?</h3><p>La ciclosporiasis es una enfermedad intestinal causada por el parásito microscópico Cyclospora. La infección a menudo ocurre tras consumir frutas y verduras frescas y puede provocar diarrea acuosa, cólicos estomacales, gases y náuseas.</p><p>El parásito, que prefiere el calor, infecta los intestinos y se propaga a través de las heces. En el pasado, las personas se han infectado al consumir frutas o verduras expuestas a agua de riego contaminada con heces.</p><h3>¿Qué está causando la ciclosporiasis en Illinois?</h3><p>No se ha identificado una fuente definitiva para los casos en Illinois, pero las autoridades de salud pública han investigado un vínculo con la lechuga iceberg. El 17 de julio, Taylor Fresh Foods, una empresa agrícola y alimentaria con sede en California, retiró voluntariamente productos de lechuga iceberg y lechuga rallada distribuidos en 27 estados, entre ellos Illinois. En otros estados, también se retiraron productos de iceberg de la marca Marketside vendidos en tiendas selectas de Walmart.</p><p>La FDA dijo el 19 de julio que las pruebas iniciales de Cyclospora en una muestra de lechuga de Taylor Farms arrojaron un resultado falso positivo. Los productos en cuestión de Taylor Farms se cultivaron en el estado mexicano de Guanajuato. La FDA alienta al público a evitar consumir cualquier producto retirado por Taylor Farms y los CDC recomiendan que quien haya comprado la lechuga retirada la tire.</p><p>El retiro voluntario ocurrió después de que el <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/cyclosporiasis/outbreaks/07-26/index.html" target="_blank" >CDC</a> identificara la lechuga rallada servida en locales de Taco Bell en Indiana, Michigan, Kentucky, Ohio y Virginia Occidental como fuente de brotes generalizados en esos estados. Taco Bell retiró la lechuga afectada de su cadena de suministro en todo el país y planeó reemplazarla en estados selectos, dijo previamente la compañía. Taylor Farms suministró lechuga a Taco Bell, según informó el New York Times.</p><p>Los CDC también están investigando otros casos de ciclosporiasis que no están relacionados con el brote nacional.</p><p>Los brotes anteriores se han vinculado a productos frescos importados, como kits de ensalada en bolsa y bayas, según el IDPH. La ciclosporiasis no se transmite de persona a persona, dijo Landon. Incluso si una persona está enferma, por lo general no se contaminan los objetos de la casa lo suficiente como para infectar a otra persona.</p><h3>¿Cuánto tiempo tarda en recuperarse?</h3><p>Las personas deben hablar con su médico sobre hacerse la prueba si presentan síntomas, para que las autoridades de salud puedan seguir rastreando el brote, comentó Gwen Biggerstaff, subdirectora de enfermedades transmitidas por alimentos, por el agua y ambientales de los CDC.</p><p>La mayoría de las personas que contraen la enfermedad se recuperan en una o dos semanas, según los CDC. Muchas pueden recuperarse con reposo y tomando abundantes líquidos, pero algunas pueden necesitar antibióticos.</p><p>Las personas pueden experimentar hinchazón, gases y deshidratación, pero rara vez presentan complicaciones adicionales.</p><p>“El problema con esta enfermedad es que puede ser persistente”, agregó Landon. “Y puedes sentirte bastante mal, y luego puedes empezar a mejorar, y luego la diarrea puede volver a aparecer”.</p><h3>¿Debo dejar de comer frutas y verduras frescas?</h3><p>Si una persona está inmunocomprometida o tiene una condición médica subyacente, debería tomar más precauciones, dijo Landon. Eso es especialmente cierto, por ejemplo, para quienes se someterán pronto a una cirugía o a tratamientos contra el cáncer.</p><p>Todos pueden seguir las pautas típicas de seguridad alimentaria, como lavarse las manos y lavar y fregar a fondo los productos frescos. Los funcionarios de salud de Illinois también sugieren:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-4f0fafa0-91cc-11f1-9c2b-6b411a1eeda5"><li>Incorporar más frutas y verduras con cáscaras o capas externas</li><li>Consumir frutas y verduras enlatadas</li><li>Mantener los productos separados de carnes crudas y mariscos</li><li>Refrigerar frutas y verduras cortadas, peladas o cocidas dentro de dos horas</li><li>Refrigerar los productos perecederos</li><li>Cocinar las verduras a al menos 158 grados Fahrenheit</li></ul><h3><b>¿Es más seguro comprar productos en mi mercado de agricultores local de Illinois? </b></h3><p>Los frutos y verduras procedentes de un productor local más pequeño probablemente tengan menos riesgo de contaminación que los alimentos de grandes fabricantes, destacó Landon. Eso es especialmente cierto si un brote se centra en un producto determinado, pero las autoridades no saben si ese es el caso esta vez.</p><p>Así que no debe asumir que no hay ningún riesgo al comprar a un vendedor local, porque cualquier granja puede contaminarse, sobre todo debido al clima actual, explicó Landon.</p><h3><b>¿Cómo está Illinois rastreando los casos? </b></h3><p>El Departamento de Salud Pública de Illinois trabaja con las autoridades de salud locales para recopilar datos sobre los casos. También trabajan con los CDC para investigar una posible fuente de la enfermedad.</p><p>El Departamento de Salud Pública de Chicago (CDPH) no ha identificado la fuente de los casos locales. Una persona había comido en Taco Bell pero también había viajado a uno de los estados que forman parte del brote mayor. El departamento está viendo un aumento de casos entre latinos que no habían viajado recientemente al extranjero.</p><p>El número de casos tanto a nivel local como en todo el país podría ser mayor, dijo Landon. Eso se debe a que las pruebas para la ciclosporiasis son caras y algunos seguros pueden no cubrirlas. Pero a medida que la ciclosporiasis aparece más en las noticias, es probable que los médicos comiencen a hacer más pruebas a los pacientes o receten antibióticos para tratarla si alguien presenta síntomas.</p><p>Si a una persona se le confirma ciclosporiasis, destacó Landon, es importante cooperar con el departamento de salud local para detallar todo lo que comió, de modo que las autoridades puedan identificar la fuente del brote.</p><h3><b>¿Los recortes federales están afectando el brote? </b></h3><p>El verano pasado, el gobierno federal redujo un programa conocido como Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network que monitoreaba las enfermedades transmitidas por alimentos, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/cdc-quietly-scaled-back-surveillance-program-foodborne-illnesses-rcna227089?link_source=ta_bluesky_link&taid=68add0b9b2316600014ce6de&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_medium=social&utm_source=bluesky" target="_blank" >informó previamente NBC News</a>. Como parte de los cambios, la notificación de parásitos Cyclospora pasó a ser opcional en 2025, según el sitio web del programa. El gobierno había recopilado esos datos desde 1997.</p><p>El programa federal reducido trabajaba con la FDA para probar proactivamente ciertos alimentos y verificar si era necesario emitir retiros, dijo Landon.</p><p>Es difícil evaluar cuánto están influyendo los cambios a nivel federal en los brotes actuales, agregó Landon. Pero es algo que los funcionarios de salud de todo el país deberían considerar.</p><p>“Es una combinación de la naturaleza de la enfermedad, el hecho de que está ocurriendo en un momento en que hay otros casos esporádicos, y luego la falta de infraestructura y recursos disponibles para las pruebas sí importa”, dijo Landon, resumiendo los factores que impulsan el brote.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Senate committee votes to hold Fauci in contempt for refusing to answer COVID questions
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON (AP) — A Senate committee voted along party lines Thursday to <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/fauci-fifth-amendment-congress-justice-department-paul-868a0dfcf016d830571fb6a78afae4f9" target="_blank" >hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress </a>over his refusal to answer questions at a hearing on his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, setting up a referral to the Department of Justice for potential investigation over whether the country’s longtime top <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/health-d9ca855cbf3589e9443a710341129681" target="_blank" >infectious disease official</a> properly exercised his constitutional rights.</p><p>The vote approving the contempt resolution came a week <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/fauci-covid19-pandemic-senate-rand-paul-a774a79e46824ebec9e8e270b9cb9825" target="_blank" >after Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right</a> against self-incrimination more than 100 times when he appeared before the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, an episode that raised fresh legal questions about the ability of Congress to compel testimony from a previously pardoned witness.</p><p>Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, the committee chairman who pressed for the contempt finding, said that constitutional protection did not apply because <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/biden-trump-fauci-milley-pardons-january-6-3cba287f89051513fb48d7ae700ae747" target="_blank" >Fauci last year received a pardon from Democratic President Joe Biden</a> and thus did not have to worry about the threat of prosecution. He has said he intends to send the referral directly to the Justice Department, rather than first to the full Senate, despite Democratic questions over the legal validity of such a maneuver.</p><p>“Dr. Fauci faced no risk of federal prosecution,” Paul said at the outset of Thursday’s hearing. “All he had to do was tell the truth.”</p><p>Fauci, in a statement last week explaining his decision to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights, said he had good reason to fear the possibility of criminal charges given what he said was Paul’s determination “to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, quote, behind bars, unquote.”</p><p>Fauci’s lawyer, David Schertler, said in a statement that the contempt resolution was “a continuation of Senator Paul’s personal vendetta against Dr. Fauci, who spent 50 years in public health and has saved countless lives.” Schertler accused Paul of abusing his power by trying to “weaponize the Justice Department.”</p><p>“Today’s partisan committee vote is a crude political stunt intended to punish Dr. Fauci for exercising his constitutional rights,” Schertler said. “The Senate should reject Senator Paul’s meritless and politically-motivated contempt resolution. For years, Senator Paul has proclaimed to anyone who would listen that Dr. Fauci should be prosecuted and put in prison. Dr. Fauci has committed no crime – and Senator Paul knows it.”</p><p>The pardon from Biden covered acts from 2014 through the January 2025 day it was issued but does not shield him from state-level prosecutions or for federal investigations into any testimony he did give that lawmakers deemed false.</p><p>Democrats who unanimously opposed the contempt resolution agreed with Fauci that he had a well-founded fear of self-incrimination given a publicly stated desire by Republicans to see him prosecuted in connection with COVID. The Trump administration has also raised questions about whether the Biden pardons were valid given Biden’s frequent use of an autopen to conduct official business.</p><p>“The goal was to wait for Dr. Fauci to make any kind of misstatement and then have a weaponized Department of Justice file criminal charges for that new statement that would not have been covered by the pardon, leaving Dr. Fauci little choice but to invoke his constitutional right to not walk directly into a trap,” said Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., before the vote.</p><p>Paul’s intention to send the referral directly to the Justice Department would leave it up to the U.S. attorney in Washington to decide whether to investigate or potentially attempt to prosecute Fauci for contempt. A referral from Congress does not compel prosecutors to act.</p><p>The committee’s top Democrat, Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, questioned whether the referral would be legally valid if Paul transmitted it to the Justice Department without the approval of the entire Senate, where the 60 votes needed to pass the resolution are seen as unlikely. He said punishing a witness for exercising a constitutional right against self-incrimination would complicate future efforts by Congress to conduct oversight and compel appearances and testimony.</p><p>“If this committee now seeks to punish a witness for asserting their (constitutionally) protected Fifth Amendment rights, future witnesses will argue that appearing before Congress exposes them to punishment regardless of whether they comply with a subpoena and invoke a constitutional protection,” he said. “They will point directly to this vote — this vote — as a justification for refusing to appear at all.”<br></p>

entries.title: ICE threatens to file criminal charges against Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart for not turning over inmates
entries.summary: <p>Federal immigration enforcement officials threatened to file criminal charges against Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart if he failed to comply with subpoenas asking his office to turn over detainees who were held at Cook County Jail.</p><p>Matt Walberg, a spokesman for the sheriff’s office, said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement sent the four subpoenas last month, along with letters threatening Dart.</p><p>The New York Times first reported that ICE had threatened to charge Dart and Dawanna S. Witt<u>,</u> the sheriff in Minnesota’s Hennepin County, which includes Minneapolis.</p><p>The counties they represent were both rocked by deportation campaigns carried out during President Donald Trump’s second term.</p><p>The administration’s tactics shifted after immigration enforcement agents <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/08/ice-shooting-minneapolis-chicago-homeland-security-immigration-deportation" target="_blank" >fatally shot two American citizens</a> in Minneapolis, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/01/28/va-nurse-vigil-alex-pretti-call-ice-border-patrol" target="_blank" >prompting outrage</a> and calls for reform. But the letters indicate the feds are still focused on Chicago and Minneapolis, which are so-called sanctuary cities that don’t cooperate with civil immigration enforcement.</p><p>Dart received separate subpoenas demanding the sheriff’s office allow four detainees to attend interviews at ICE’s offices in the Loop, or to bring them in upon their release. Three had already been released from the county jail, Walberg said. </p><p>An attached letter said failure to comply with the subpoena “may constitute Tampering with a Witness … and, if convicted, may result in fines and a term of imprisonment.” </p><p>Walberg said the sheriff’s office is required to keep detainees in custody and can’t release them for interviews with other law enforcement agencies or turn them over when they’re released.</p><p>Sheriff Witt issued a statement saying the threats of prosecution she received “will not cause me to abandon my legal responsibilities or disregard constitutional protections. My focus remains on doing my job lawfully and not responding to political pressure or intimidation."</p><p>Witt’s spokeswoman, Rebecca Aurelious, said the office also received subpoenas for detainees who had already been released from custody.</p><p>A U.S. Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said it’s common practice to subpoena local law enforcement officials who “refused to cooperate with federal immigration authorities and detainers.” The spokesperson said the tactic had also been used during Trump’s first term.</p><p>“We’re continuing these efforts as sanctuary politicians refuse to hand over the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens,” the spokesperson said. “Non-cooperative jurisdictions have a choice: stop harboring criminal illegal aliens and releasing them into their communities, or work with ICE to make America safe again.</p><p>“Either way, ICE will not be slowing down on enforcing federal law.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/08/ice-shooting-minneapolis-chicago-homeland-security-immigration-deportation" target="_blank" >ICE shooting in Minneapolis echoes what feds did in Chicago</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/01/28/va-nurse-vigil-alex-pretti-call-ice-border-patrol" target="_blank" >Hundreds honor Alex Pretti, call for abolition of ICE and Chicagoans to join nationwide general strike</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Review: Jane Schoenbrun’s ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ turns slasher tropes inward
entries.summary: <p>It was an unexpected turn of events after seeing Jane Schoenbrun's buzzy third feature “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.”which received its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/07/09/mubi-fest-chicago-teenage-death-at-camp-miasma-lurker" target="_blank" >Chicago premiere at Mubi Fest in July</a>. Suddenly, after nearly 30 years of not thinking about the Counting Crows, their 1996 ballad “A Long December” was firmly stuck in my head, and it wouldn’t go away.</p><p>The film itself, a playful pastiche of shlocky, problematic slasher films, and send-up of the pressure to create within the confines of Hollywood reboot culture, had not left me especially transported. It seemed, at first, like something that had been made expressly for film snobs and critics, the kind that flatters insider knowledge, niche fandoms and unabashed love of bad movies, a self-consciously styled cult classic in the making. But I couldn’t stop thinking about that song, and the strangely sublime sequence that accompanies it. “A Long December” was so ubiquitous when I was around 12 and 13 that it barely even registered as something to be moved by. I had no warm nostalgia for it; it was a song that I knew simply because it was there.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.0" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-490000" name="module-490000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">“Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” a Mubi release in limited release Friday, is rated R by the Motion Picture Association for “bloody violence, gore, sexual content, graphic nudity, drug use and some language.” Running time: 106 minutes. </div> </div><p>And yet in the context of “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” a movie that I wasn’t even sure I liked very much at the time, in which it accompanies a pivotal and profound moment of carnage and catharsis, I fell in love with it. For weeks, it’s been playing on repeat in my head. This might seem like a weirdly small detail to focus on, but it was my truthful entry point to reconsidering a movie that is so personal to its filmmaker that it’s difficult to know how to even approach a review.</p><p>Schoenbrun is the most high-profile trans director working now and much of the heartbreak, horror and humor of that is embedded in “Camp Miasma” in which Hannah Einbinder plays Kris, a “Sundance wunderkind” director who has been hired to reboot a 1980s horror franchise and wants to recruit the original final girl Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson) for the project.</p><p><b></b> Kris is very much a Schoenbrun stand-in, from the fact of being Sundance breakouts down to the styling and the glasses. There is a cruel irony in the fact that Kris, who is queer, has been handed the keys to the fictional “Camp Miasma” series which are famously transphobic. The killer, called Little Death (Jack Haven), is a trans kid who was murdered and who rises out of the lake to slaughter unsuspecting campers. But Kris has always been drawn to the franchise, despite and maybe because of its problematic nature; it might have been bad for her, but it was formative nonetheless, like the big-brand candies she’s always buying at gas stations.</p><p>And Kris is on a mission to find Billy, the wide-eyed star of the original film (Amanda Fix as young Billy), who retreated from acting and now lives a solitary, reclusive life at the camp where the movie was shot. Anderson plays the older Billy as a kind of "it’s the pictures that got small" Norma Desmond-type, swanning around in bejeweled turbans, silky robes and furs and speaking in a dramatic southern/mid-Atlantic accent that, while incongruous with the idea of a one-time final girl, is enjoyable for its heightened camp, nonetheless. In reality Billy has faded into a footnote; Kris’ agent (a funny Sarah Sherman) barely knows who she is.</p><p>But nothing is quite real or especially believable in “Camp Miasma;” it’s more of a collection of feelings, tropes, styles, ideas and actors that Schoenbrun evidently loves, from Patrick Fischler, as a foreboding convenience store employee, and Dylan Baker, as a blustering Hollywood executive, to Eva Victor and Zach Cherry as some of the ill-fated camp counselors in the movie-within-the-movie who spend some of their last moments ecstatically dancing to Sally Shapiro. At a certain point you may be surprised to find that you’re fully watching a large portion of the original “Camp Miasma” along with Kris and Billy before both anti-realities bleed together to form a wild climax. This is a movie that is ultimately about sex, titillation and orgasm, after all. Even the killer's name, Little Death, is a nod to the French expression. <b></b></p><p>What “Camp Miasma” is not really is a grisly slasher. Instead, it's a thoughtfully constructed fever dream that wears its high and low-brow references on its sleeve — a bold and worthy vision that continues Schoenbrun's exploration of transitioning using the cinematic and pop cultural tools at their disposal and reinventing them in their image.</p><p>Now, excuse me, I must go listen to “A Long December” again.</p>

entries.title: John Damore, oldest living former Chicago Bears player, has died at 92
entries.summary: <p>At the peak of a 2025-26 Chicago Bears season that had fans thinking of a championship, John Damore dreamed of his "greatest goodbye" — that he might die soon after the Bears won the Super Bowl.</p><p>Mr. Damore — believed to be the oldest former Bears player since January 2025 — died Tuesday at home in Westmont. He was 92.</p><p>His dream didn't come true for the Bears, eliminated by the Los Angeles Rams.</p><p>"There weren’t many people out there who didn’t just think he was the super-nicest guy," Larry Damore said of his father. "He always had a crowd around him." </p><p>Mr. Damore grew up in Riverside and remembered wearing a Bears jersey as a 9-year-old, long before he'd wear the team's colors as an offensive lineman in 1957 and 1959.</p><p>An ankle injury prompted him to retire in 1959. But Mr. Damore's love for the Bears only deepened. In an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/01/07/john-damore-oldest-chicago-bears-super-bowl" >interview last year with the Chicago Sun-Times,</a> he spoke of spending every game day on his bedroom recliner, with an unlit cigar in hand and his eyes glued to the Bears on TV.</p><p>“I don’t miss a minute," he said. "And, if it plays twice, I watch it twice.”</p><p>Larry Damore said, as a kid, he wrestled and played football and baseball, with his father often coaching him but always there.</p><p>"He never missed a game," he said. "He was always leading the cheers."</p><p>John Bihun, a grandson, said he remembers a T-ball game at which Mr. Damore said he could "die a happy man" if he got to see him hit a home run. </p><p>Bihun said that, as he rounded third base after hitting the ball, his grandfather shouted, "I didn’t mean today, Lord!" </p><p>Mr. Damore, a Marine Corps veteran, formerly owned Damore Construction and Damore Builders in Riverside.</p><p>He is survived by his wife of 65 years, Joyce Damore, children Alison Bihun and Lawrence “Larry” Damore and grandchildren John Bihun and Ashley Bihun. </p><p>Visitation will be from 3 p.m. to 8 p.m. Aug. 19 at Conboy-Westchester Funeral Home in Westchester, with a service there at 10 a.m. Aug. 20.</p><p><i>Contributing: Mary Norkol</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/01/18/bears-rams-john-damore-nfl-football-sports" >Watching the cardiac Rams-Bears game with oldest living Bears alum John Damore</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/01/07/john-damore-oldest-chicago-bears-super-bowl" >Oldest living Chicago Bear, 92, hopes team has Super Bowl in its future: ‘It would be my greatest goodbye’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Joven de 16 años que viajaba en scooter muere atropellado por un camión en la Avenida Western
entries.summary: <p>Un adolescente de 16 años que iba en un scooter eléctrico fue atropellado mortalmente por un conductor de camión en North Center el lunes, convirtiéndose en el tercer adolescente muerto en un accidente de tráfico relacionado con patines eléctricos este año.</p><p>El joven circulaba hacia el norte por la cuadra 4100 al norte de Western Avenue alrededor de las 3:35 p.m. cuando perdió el control y fue alcanzado por un camión de carga, dijo la Policía de Chicago en un comunicado. Fue trasladado al Illinois Masonic Hospital, donde fue declarado muerto, informó la policía.</p><p>También comunicó que se esperaba la emisión de multas y la investigación continúa.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3e0000" name="module-3e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El joven, Alex Blacio, iba de regreso a casa del trabajo, según una <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/ayuda-para-funeral-de-alex" target="_blank" >página de GoFundMe</a> creada para la familia del joven.</p><p>Los choques relacionados con scooters han aumentado junto con el incremento de usuarios en los últimos años, lo que ha motivado una <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/05/04/chicago-launches-e-scooter-safety-campaign-in-wake-of-recent-scooter-deaths" target="_blank" >campaña de seguridad</a> de la Ciudad. El Departamento de Bomberos de Chicago respondió a casi 200 incidentes relacionados con patines eléctricos en 2022. Esa cifra se había <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/06/05/scooter-escooters-lane-tech-safety-teenagers-crashes" target="_blank" >triplicado más de una vez para 2025</a>.</p><p>Los scooters eléctricos se han vuelto cada vez más populares entre los estudiantes de Lane Tech College Prep, a menos de una milla al sur del lugar del choque.</p><p>Hasta ahora este año, otros dos adolescentes han sido atropellados fatalmente por conductores mientras iban en patines eléctricos: la venezolana de 17 años <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/05/01/loved-ones-launch-fundraiser-for-venezuelan-teenager-killed-in-south-side-scooter-crash" target="_blank" >Astrid Alexandra Carrillo Noguera</a> y la adolescente de 15 años <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/girl-15-killed-while-riding-scooter-in-south-shore-hit-and-run" target="_blank" >Violet Harris</a> fueron ambas víctimas de accidentes esta primavera en el lado sur con casi un mes de diferencia.</p><p>Seis personas que iban en scooters o bicicletas fueron <a class="Link" href="https://api.chicago.gov/filenet5/servlets/getDocumentContent?applicationId=CompleteStreets&documentId=%7B601CB99F-0000-C917-A80A-59C827820B0F%7D" target="_blank" >atropelladas mortalmente por automóviles</a> entre enero y junio de este año, comparado a una persona en el mismo período del año pasado. El número de muertes por tráfico —que la Ciudad había prometido eliminar para este año— <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/08/25/vision-zero-traffic-crash-deaths-pedestrian-cyclist-car-roads-streets" target="_blank" >permanece, en gran medida, donde estaba hace 10 años</a> tras un breve aumento durante la pandemia.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Family of Marine veteran killed in Fox River crash files wrongful death suit
entries.summary: <p>The family of a woman killed in a boat crash on the Fox River last month has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the man who caused it.</p><p>Magdalena Jablonska, of Des Plaines, was out on the river with her fiance, Alan Telmini, and their dog, Sasha, on July 25 when they were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/30/family-mourns-des-plaines-woman-killed-in-boat-crash-over-the-weekend" target="_blank" >hit by a speeding boat </a>while in a “no wake zone" in suburban McHenry. </p><p>“I heard loud engines. I moved to the left of Maggie and then she was gone,” said Telmini at a news conference Thursday. “I relive that moment every day.”</p><p>Richard Stevenson, 45, was driving his pontoon while intoxicated at an “extremely high rate of speed” before he crashed into the couple who had stopped to eat lunch around 2:30 p.m., according to family and the McHenry County State’s Attorney’s office.</p><p>Jablonska, 48, suffered blunt-force injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene, said the McHenry County Coroner’s office. Telmini was injured and was taken to a nearby hospital. Sasha was uninjured.</p><p>Stevenson, whose blood alcohol level was nearly three times the legal limit, was found in the trees off the shoreline near where his pontoon had come to rest. He was taken into custody, prosecutors said, and charged with one count of reckless homicide and two counts of aggravated DUI causing death.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </div><p>Jablonska’s family says they want justice.</p><p>“She used to say everything happens for a reason but this didn’t have to happen,” said Michelle Macias, Jablonska’s younger sister, at the had a duty to operate his boat safely but instead acted recklessly, causing Jablonska's death and endangering others on the river.</p><p>Telmini said they just wanted to “enjoy their day” when they went out on the river, which was something the couple did often in summer. He said there were several boaters on the river that day.</p><p>“We want to see justice,” he said, "that other people are going to be safe on the river.”</p><p>Jablonska's family is suing Stevenson for wrongful death, personal injuries and negligent infliction of emotional distress.</p><p>Stevenson has a history of arrests for driving a motor vehicle under the influence. He had previously been charged on three occasions with DUI, reckless driving and speeding. After graduating from high school, she joined the Marine Corps and was stationed in Okinawa.</p><p>Jablonska later got a job working at Servpro, handling insurance claims. She also served as treasurer of the Women Marine Association, IL-2 Blanche S. Osborne Chapter.</p><p>“The bond between Marines is lifelong,” said Ann Crittenden, national president of WMA, in a statement. “Though Maggie's watch has ended far too soon, the impact she made through her service, friendship, and commitment to her fellow Marines will remain with us always.”<br></p>

entries.title: Jalapeños linked to a U.S. salmonella outbreak tracked to a Mexican farm, distributor
entries.summary: <p>(AP) — Jalapeño peppers linked to a <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/chipotle-jalapeno-salmonella-outbreak-investigation-feecdd5ba46237c8992e41de8ea6d1df" target="_blank" >multistate salmonella outbreak</a> have been traced back to a grower in Sinaloa, Mexico, federal officials say.</p><p>At least 345 people in 27 states have been reported getting sick from the salmonella strain linked to the jalapeños. Most have been in Minnesota and Colorado. No deaths have been reported, but officials say 36 people have been hospitalized.</p><p>The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Wednesday that the chili peppers were moved into the U.S. by Coast Citrus Distributors. The company has recalled the peppers and is notifying its customers, which include some prominent Mexican food restaurant chains, officials said.</p><p>Coast Citrus Distributors didn't immediately respond to a Thursday voicemail seeking comment.</p><p>The Food and Drug Administration said that of the 191 people interviewed in the outbreak investigation, 177 — or 93% — reported eating at a Mexican-style restaurant, including Chipotle Mexican Grill and Qdoba, from June 14 to July 14.</p><p>Chipotle Mexican Grill said Tuesday that it had removed jalapeños from some of its restaurants. Qdoba on Wednesday said the company had proactively removed jalapenos from all of its restaurants.</p><p>“Given their actions to remove product from their stores, neither of these establishments are considered a current ongoing risk to consumers in this outbreak,” CDC officials said in a statement.</p><p>The FDA is investigating whether any of the jalapeños went to grocery stores. The agency may announce more actions on its <a class="Link" href="https://www.fda.gov/safety/recalls-market-withdrawals-safety-alerts" target="_blank" >recalls webpage</a>, health officials said.</p><p>Salmonella bacteria cause about 1.35 million infections in the United States every year, and outbreaks have <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/salmonella/outbreaks/index.html" target="_blank" >been tied</a> to sources such as <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/salmonella-cucumbers-outbreak-florida-water-fccb66a1e0733fc97d29065e287052bc" target="_blank" >cucumbers</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/salmonella-cucumbers-sunfed-fda-fd58db35645ce8302d2211035b67dc90" target="_blank" >eggs</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/raw-milk-salmonella-bird-flu-raw-farm-99c8c79ece9bc2a9f90dc4f917292dad" target="_blank" >unpasteurized milk</a>, fresh basil, geckos and pet bearded dragons.</p><p>Within hours or days of being exposed to the bacteria, infected people can suffer from diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps. The illness usually lasts four to seven days, and most people recover without treatment.</p><p>Young children, retirement-age adults and people with weakened immune systems are at higher risk for more severe illness, according to the CDC.</p><p>Shares of Chipotle, based in Newport Beach, California, tumbled nearly 10% Tuesday and have not recovered. A number of fast-casual chains like Chipotle have seen less foot traffic from middle- and lower-income customers due to broader inflation in the U.S., and recent headlines about <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/cyclospora-lettuce-taco-bell-restaurants-customers-39083c579b4ba7d3d5d8a23ea3fd5b00" target="_blank" >foodborne illnesses</a> may be another negative.<br></p>

entries.title: Bears Training Camp Report, Day 8: QB Caleb Williams sharper
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ physical Thursday <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/06/bears-training-camp-braxton-jones-leaves-practice-injury-ben-johnson-left-tackle" target="_blank" >training camp practice</a>:</p><h3><b>What happened</b></h3><p>Quarterback Caleb Williams was much sharper than he was Tuesday, the last time the Bears held a padded practice. He finished Thursday’s session with a 4-yard touchdown pass to Luther Burden along the back of the end zone to cap a two-minute drill in which he went 6-for-6 for 60 yards. The offense started the drill at their own 35 with 1:41 to play and trailing by three.</p><p>Earlier, Williams threw a 43-yard touchdown pass to Rome Odunze in which Odunze caught the pass, bounced off safety Cam Lewis and sprinted down the field.<br>He threw an interception to cornerback Tyrique Stevenson, though Stevenson fumbled the ball away to the offense on his return run.</p><h3>Cairo kicks</h3><p>Cairo Santos went a perfect 6-for-6 in field goal drills, making kicks ranging from 33 yards to 56 yards. It was the best day of camp for the 34-year-old kicker, whose leg strength seems to be better than ever.</p><h3><b>Watching</b></h3><p>Bulls executive vice president of football operations Bryson Graham visited practice and chatted with Bears GM Ryan Poles.</p><h3><b>What’s next?</b></h3><p>The Bears have Friday off before returning for practice at 8:30 a.m. Saturday at Halas Hall.<br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Bears LT Braxton Jones, DE Montez Sweat leave practice with injury
entries.summary: <p>Less than two hours after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson said he hoped to have “clarity” at his starting left tackle spot by the middle of next week, things got murky again.</p><p>Braxton Jones, the overwhelming favorite to win the job, walked off the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/06/bears-training-camp-report-day-8-qb-caleb-williams-sharper-bryson-graham-nfl-bulls" target="_blank" >practice</a> field Thursday with trainer Andre Tucker after getting hurt during one-on-one drills against defensive end Austin Booker.</p><p>Jones lined up against Booker on consecutive reps; after the first, the two stayed entangled for a few seconds, leaving Jones frustrated. It's unclear whether he was hurt during the play or the brief skirmish.</p><p>After the second rep, an emotional Jones ripped off his own helmet and chucked it into the bushes that line the back entrance to Halas Hall. Offensive line coach Dan Roushar raced to his side and muttered a few words of encouragement. Jones paced for about five minutes and appeared to be stretching out his left leg. He did a pass set against air. Then he followed the trainer inside.</p><p>After practice, sources said Jones and the Bears were cautiously optimistic that he avoided any long-term injury. Tests are continuing.</p><p>Even if Jones misses just a few days, the Bears can’t afford to lose anyone at that position — or defensive end, either, for that matter. Montez Sweat, the team’s best edge rusher, pulled up during an 11-on-11 drill Thursday. He soon left the field with a trainer, too.</p><p>Sweat was replaced by a combination of Daniel Hardy, who plays mostly special teams, and Dayo Odeyingbo. Kiran Amegadjie played first-team left tackle snaps after Jones left.</p><p>The Bears could have added a veteran at either spot this offseason, but chose not to. Five-and-half weeks before their opener, it’s always starting to hurt them.</p><p>Later in practice, two Bears suffered ugly injuries. Safety Gervarrius Owens was carted off the field after hurting his leg during a punt drill. Chicago-born cornerback Dallis Flowers appeared to hurt his left leg. Johnson and players checked on him before he left with a trainer. Both appeared to be in considerable pain.</p><p>Slot cornerback Jaylon Jones, who was playing with the starters because of injuries to cornerback Kyler Gordon and safety Coby Bryant, didn’t finish practice, either. Receiver Kalif Raymond was shaken up on the last play of practice, but declared himself fine.</p><p><b>"</b>A little bit better," he said, "now that it’s over."</p><p>At two hours and 10 minutes, Thursday’s practice was the Bears’ longest of camp. Wedged between Wednesday’s walk-through and Friday’s day off, it was the most physical— though it felt short of the grueling, tempo-setting session Johnson steered last season. That day is likely coming later. Practice began with a 9-on-7 drill in which the offense, playing short-handed, blocked running plays. The drill was so nasty that linebacker D’Marco Jackson had to have his facemask replaced.</p><p>Jones’ injury happened, cruelly, about two hours after Johnson said he’d hoped to clarify his left tackle job next week. The Bears seem to be leading toward Jones starting — since the team began practicing in pads, he’s taken more snaps with the first team than Jedrick Wills or Amegadjie.</p><p>When Johnson said he hoped to have clarity this week, he vowed to “continue to cycle guys through” at practice.</p><p>That’s what happened last year. Jones began the season at left tackle before being replaced by Theo Benedet. Ozzy Trapilo, a second-round pick, then emerged as the starter before hurting his patellar tendon in the playoff win against the Packers. Rather than start Jones against the Rams, the Bears moved guard Joe Thuney to tackle.</p><p>This year, the Bears want to know their starter at the position as soon as possible. Jones’ injury complicates that.</p><p>“We'll go as long as we need to,” Johnson said. “And even if that means into the season, we'll do whatever it takes.”</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Bears' Ben Johnson, Cole Kmet, Colston Loveland to appear in Hallmark Channel movie
entries.summary: <p>Ben Johnson made his acting debut over the summer when he filmed a brief appearance in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>-themed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/13/hallmark-holiday-touchdown-bears-love-story-christkindlmarket" target="_blank" >Hallmark Channel</a> movie.</p><p>Two of Johnson’s players appear in “Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story,” which will premiere Oct. 17 on the Hallmark Channel. Tight ends Colston Loveland and Cole Kmet have a small role in the movie. All three are playing themselves.</p><p>Johnson, who had never acted before, joked Thursday morning that he and Kmet "took a lot of acting classes this offseason — so we were ready for this."</p><p>Loveland was fine without the sessions, he deadpanned.</p><p>"He did not need them," he said. "It was natural."</p><p>Two Pro Football Hall of Famers — Dan Hampton and Mike Singletary — and beloved former Bears cornerback Charles Tillman will be in the TV movie. Connie Payton, Walter’s widow, has a part, too, the team announced Wednesday.</p><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Get ready to see some familiar faces in Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story premiering Saturday October 17 on Hallmark Channel, streaming next day on Hallmark Plus! 🤩 <a href="https://t.co/UvJvhIo6op">pic.twitter.com/UvJvhIo6op</a></p>— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears/status/2085064130327715894?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 5, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The movie stars Lyndsy Fonseca and Robert Buckley and features Marsha Mason, Khary Payton and Barbara Alyn Woods. Marilu Henner, Tamera Mowry-Housley, Dyon “Mojo” Brooks and Jake Connelly will make cameos.</p><p>The movie was filmed entirely in Chicago. The Bears’ scenes were shot at Soldier Field, Halas Hall and downtown. Last month, crews filmed the Christmas-themed movie at a reconstructed Christkindlmarket.</p><p></p><p>The Bears are the third NFL team to participate in a “Holiday Touchdown” movie, joining the Bills and Chiefs. Andy Reid, the Chiefs’ coach, and Sean McDermott, the Bills’ coach, each appeared in their team’s respective movies.</p>

Steelworkers Local 7-1 have been locked out of BP's sprawling plant in Whiting, Indiana, without pay and with no clear indication of when they'll return to work. During a lockout, management can prevent workers from returning to their jobs to withhold wages.</p><p><b>New playbook?</b>: Lockouts are generally seen as a hardline tactic during labor disputes and tend to be rare, especially in the refining business, which requires continuous production and a highly skilled workforce. Longtime refinery workers worry Big Oil is experimenting with a new playbook to break union power, undermine national collective bargaining, and remake its workforce.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: This year, 98% of USW Local 7-1 members voted to reject what the fossil fuel company called its last, best, and final offer. The company then issued a lockout order. The proposal would have held up wages, cut jobs, and expanded the use of artificial intelligence, according to the union. </p><p><b>BP's response</b>: In a statement to WBEZ, BP objected to the union's characterization of its demands and said most of what it's seeking has "already been tested and implemented elsewhere" — and the lockout "allowed for a safe and orderly transition of operations."</p><p><b>Pritzker writes oil CEOs</b>: In other oil news, Gov. target="_blank" >Jewél Jackson</a></h5><h5></h5><p><b>Block club breakdown</b>: Block clubs are coalitions of neighbors who volunteer to improve the physical and social conditions of their block. That can range from planting flowers on the parkway to buying abandoned homes in order to increase the neighborhood’s market value. These clubs differ from homeowners associations because they are not legally mandated for residents to participate in or pay fees toward.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: During the Great Migration of the early 20th century, the Chicago Urban League provided financial and community support to new arrivals, including helping to form block clubs. Today, you'll still see evidence of block clubs in South and West Side neighborhoods: colorful signs, often wooden and hand-painted.</p><p><b>Chicagoan's POV</b>: West Garfield Park resident Helen King has been a member of the Westside Block Club Association for decades. href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuuduht-l-il/" target="_blank" >Chicago State prepares to make history as Division I football returns to Chicago</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuuduht-l-ir/" target="_blank" >Elijah James</a></h5><p>Players cycled through warm-ups, worked at individual position drills and scrimmaged under the watchful eyes of coaches and gathered media Wednesday at Chicago State University.</p><p>It was a lot like any other media day for most Division I football programs. Except this was Chicago State University, and it has never had a football team before. Wednesday's open practice at the Emil and Patricia A. Jones Convocation Center was a milestone for both the university and the city. </p><p>The Cougars, playing in the Football Championship Subdivision, will become the first Division I football team to call the city home since the University of Chicago last fielded a Division I team in 1939. After that season, U of C famously shut down its program and left the Big Ten; that school now competes in Division III.</p><p>Offensive line coach Arthur Ray Jr., a Mount Carmel High School graduate, said the significance of the program extends beyond the football field. He views it as an opportunity to establish a Division I team that truly belongs to the city.</p><p>"Chicago's a sports city, and we’re building the next great sports platform at a Division I university right on the South Side," Ray said. "We're truly Chicago’s only Division I team. You ain't got to go far, we're right down the street from Old Fashioned Donuts, Harold's down the street on 87th. This is real Chicago, real South Side."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuuduht-l-iy/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>Have you ever been part of a block club in your community? entries.title: Did Sam Antonacci give Willson Contreras a chicken wing?
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — Did the White Sox’ Sam Antonacci give the Red Sox’ Willson Contreras a chicken wing at first base Wednesday?</p><p>It depends who you ask.</p><p>The question arose Thursday morning when well-known Red Sox fan Bill Simmons posted a video of the two players converging on X with the message, “I still can’t believe Contreras didn’t kill this guy.” It has more than 1 millions views.</p><p>Contreras certainly thought so, just by his reaction. White Sox manager Will Venable admitted the “optics” weren’t good. The Sun-Times asked Antonacci before the game Thursday night whether he intended to give the Red Sox firstbaseman a chicken wing as he ran by.</p><p>“Just running through,” he said.</p><p>Are you sure?</p><p>“Yes, sir.”</p><p>The video tells a different story.</p><p>Antonacci hit a bouncer to Contreras, who fielded the ball and ran to touch the bag with his left foot, beating a hustling Antonacci. After touching the base, Contreras took two steps away from the bag, heading toward pitcher Sonny Gray.</p><p>That’s when Antonacci appeared to knock Contreras’ left elbow with his left elbow. Contreras stopped, turned around and looked at Antonacci. TV cameras caught Contreras looking at Antonacci and saying, “You OK?” Anontacci didn’t appear to look back or say anything as he ran by toward the third-base dugout.</p><p>Contreras, a former Cubs catcher, has been involved in many incidents in his 11-year career, and he even has sought some out. But he didn’t appear to be at fault here. Contreras left the game in the fifth inning with an illness, and he wasn’t in the Red Sox’ clubhouse during media availability Thursday.</p><p>Simmons’ take wasn’t wrong. Contreras runs hot. But he stayed cool in this case, even appearing to give a thumbs-up and a wave toward the White Sox’ dugout before returning to his position. It’s rare for Contreras to demonstrate such restraint.</p><p>This season alone, he has been involved in a couple of incidents, including one that got him suspended for five games, down from the initial ruling of seven. In June against the Nationals, Contreras got into a jawing match with pitcher Cade Cavalli that led to a benches-clearing brawl. Contreras later apologized, saying the recent earthquakes in Venezuela were weighing on him.</p><p>There’s a list of incidents at first base of similar nature in baseball history. A famous one involved the Red Sox in the 2004 American League Championship Series, when the Yankees’ Alex Rodriguez slapped the ball out of pitcher Bronson Arroyo’s glove on his way to first base. After conferring, the umpires ruled him out.</p><p>In a 2003 National League Division Series at Wrigley Field, the Braves’ Robert Fick threw a forearm into Cubs first baseman Eric Karros’ arm and glove, knocking away the ball and glove. Needing no discussion, the umpires called Fick out immediately, and Major League Baseball later fined him.</p><p>But Antonacci was already out when he made contact with Contreras. And from the view of the camera aimed up the first-base line, it sure looked like Antonacci wasn’t “just running through.”</p><p>Two innings later, with Antonacci on second base, Miguel Vargas hit a grounder to third baseman Caleb Durbin, whose throw pulled Contreras off the bag. That had Antonacci thinking he could score, but Contreras’ throw got to catcher Connor Wong in plenty of time.</p><p>Karma’s a you-know-what.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module entries.title: Cubs’ best-in-baseball glovework has pitchers jazzed to join: ‘This is the defense you want to pitch behind’
entries.summary: <p>A legitimate shot at October glory and the electric atmosphere at Wrigley Field are selling points, sure.</p><p>But what excites pitchers more than anything about coming to the Cubs?</p><p>“I’ll tell you, I’m pretty excited to pitch with this defense behind me,” right-hander <b>Kevin Gausman</b> said Wednesday. “I’m really looking forward to that.”</p><p><b>Jed Hoyer</b>’s front office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >got aggressive at the trade deadline</a>, bringing in needed pitching to fortify a Cubs roster built for the postseason.</p><p>That pitching looks capable of helping the Cubs to a deep October run, not only because the likes of Gausman and fellow righty starter <b>Clay Holmes</b> are effective weapons on the mound, but because they get to pitch in front of the best defense in baseball.</p><p>“For me, this defense, this is one of the best places I could have come,” Holmes said Tuesday. “People around the league, you know the Cubs got a really good defense. You see them play, and it’s special.</p><p>“A guy like me, that’s what I do. I’m a sinker-ball guy, [and I] rely on the quality of contact. To be able to trust a defense like that and know that’s what you have behind you is a freeing thing.”</p><p>The field is littered with Gold Glovers – five of them, to be exact, in second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner</b>, shortstop <b>Dansby Swanson</b>, third baseman <b>Alex Bregman</b>, left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> and center fielder <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> – and even those without that lustrous hardware are plenty capable of making stellar plays, just look at what infielder <b>Pedro Ramirez</b> and right fielder <b>Seiya Suzuki</b> did earlier this week against the Dodgers.</p><p>The Cubs have a reputation as a place where if a pitcher can keep the ball in the ballpark, it’s going to get gobbled up by an elite defender. And the numbers back up the reputation, too, with the Cubs tops in the sport in numerous statistical categories.</p><p>“We’ve got a really good defense,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Wednesday. “It is true, if you’re a pitcher, this is the defense you want to pitch behind. Hopefully, a lot of pitchers are recognizing that.”</p><p>The team’s newly arrived arms are thrilled to go to work.</p><p>“It allows you to be in attack mode in every situation,” Gausman said. “You feel like no matter what’s going to happen, the outcome’s usually going to be on your side.”</p><p><b>Rehabbing pitchers</b></p><p>A trio of injured Cubs hurlers made minor league rehab appearances with Triple-A Iowa on Wednesday.</p><p>Righty starter <b>Edward Cabrera</b>, working back from a hamstring strain, pitched four scoreless innings. Lefty reliever <b>Hoby Milner</b>, out since a late-June appendectomy, faced six hitters and gave up a run. And righty reliever <b>Daniel Palencia</b>, coming back from elbow inflammation, retired just two of the five hitters he faced, allowing a hit and two walks.</p><p>All three are slated for more minor league rehab work before returning to the big league team.</p><p><b>Another deadline add arrives</b></p><p>The Cubs brought lefty pitcher <b>Braxton Garrett</b>, acquired in a Monday trade with the Marlins, up from Triple-A Iowa ahead of Thursday’s game.</p><p>“He’s a name we’ve talked about here for a while, not just this year at the trade deadline,” pitching coach <b>Tommy Hottovy</b> said. “The role of coming in and being in the bullpen right now is a lot more for us to have some protection. I think long term, he’s definitely a guy we see who can start and be a good starter in the big leagues. Where we are in the season, though, that obviously changes things for this year.”</p>

entries.title: Clutch Cubs victorious on Alex Bregman blast, Pete Crow-Armstrong steal: ‘Good teams find ways to win’
entries.summary: <p>Two outs. Two strikes. Two runs to get.</p><p>And Alex Bregman got ‘em.</p><p>The two-time World Series winner and $175 million <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> signee hasn’t produced like he’s wanted to this season, but the ball he dropped into the basket for a game-tying home run Thursday probably made a lot of fans suddenly feel like he was worth every penny.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">ALEX BREGMAN!<br><br>The <a href="https://x.com/Cubs?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Cubs</a> tie the game down to their final strike! <a href="https://t.co/M1RUOaYc8C">pic.twitter.com/M1RUOaYc8C</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2085473712053113130?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 6, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“That’s a huge hit. That means everything,” manager Craig Counsell said. “That’s one that takes an ‘L’ off the board and gets you a ‘W.’”</p><p>The third baseman’s bat is coming to life, and he could win over every North Side skeptic down the stretch of this pennant race, as the lights get brighter and his winning experience becomes all the more valuable.</p><p>But it will be difficult for him to come up with a bigger hit than this one, a down-to-their-last-strike homer in the bottom of the ninth inning that kept Thursday’s bout with the Blue Jays going long enough for the Cubs to score a 3-2 walk-off, extra-inning win.</p><p>“That’s who Alex Bregman is, man,” center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong said. “He’s shown people that he’s built for those moments. He just showed people again that that is where he belongs and where he thrives.”</p><p>Prior to the ninth inning, the Cubs did next to nothing offensively, smothered in seven scoreless innings by Jays righty Dylan Cease, who allowed just two singles and added 10 strikeouts to his AL-leading total.</p><p>But Crow-Armstrong led off the ninth with a base hit before Bregman’s basket-shot sparked extras, where Crow-Armstrong – <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/02/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-player-of-the-month-june-stats-babe-ruth-lou-gehrig-shohei-ohtani" >serenaded with “M-V-P” chants</a> – used his speed to steal third, force an errant throw and scamper home for the game-winning run.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr"><a href="https://x.com/hashtag/WALKOFF?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#WALKOFF</a>!<br><br>Pete Crow-Armstrong races home to complete a comeback W for the <a href="https://x.com/Cubs?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Cubs</a>! <a href="https://t.co/JB9FEH7VKL">pic.twitter.com/JB9FEH7VKL</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2085481972478927007?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 6, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Another walk-off win at Wrigley, the Cubs’ 11th of the season.</p><p>“That’s my style of play,” Crow-Armstrong said, “but we’re all getting to see me do a little bit of everything more often now.”</p><p>If Bregman is just starting to show that he’s the impact player the Cubs paid for – he’s hitting .370 with a 1.082 OPS in his last 11 games – then Crow-Armstrong is finding new ways to show what he’s been doing all season long.</p><p>A day after going back and forth with Dodgers two-way star Shohei Ohtani <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/05/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-shohei-ohtani-nl-mvp-race-dodgers-playoffs-craig-counsell-shota-imanaga" >in a real-time MVP race</a>, he showed again how capable he is of making an Ohtani-esque, multi-faceted impact, not just hitting at an elite level, not just playing elite defense, but putting pressure on the opposition with an elite base-running ability.</p><p>“It’s game-changing,” Bregman said of Crow-Armstrong’s impact on the base paths. “You walk him, it’s a double. He can steal third. He can score from first. He does it in every area of the game.”</p><p>“That’s why we’re talking about Pete so much,” Counsell said, “because it’s every facet of the game he can do it in. That’s just so rare in the game.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong might be driving the bus as a legitimate threat to Ohtani’s grip on the MVP, and Bregman might end up the middle-of-the-order presence the Cubs hoped. But this team has looked so good this summer because it’s more than just one or two guys.</p><p>On a day when the bats fell silent until the last possible moment, it was pitching and the always-present defense keeping things close. Lefty starter David Peterson put a lot of guys on base but only allowed one run. The bullpen tossed six innings of one-run ball.</p><p>At the end of a home stand that threw the likes of Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Tarik Skubal and Dylan Cease at these Cubs, they walked off Thursday to cap a stretch of games in which they definitively proved they could <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/04/cubs-dodgers-three-peat-world-series-favorites-tarik-skubal-dansby-swanson" >not just hang with the game’s best but beat them</a>.</p><p>Maybe, as their record indicates, they’re one of the game’s best, too?</p><p>“Good teams find ways to win ballgames,” Bregman said. “We faced some of the best pitching in the world this home stand. I felt like our pitchers went toe to toe with them and our offense put together good at-bats.</p><p>“This home stand, we played good ball, just team ball all around in all the phases of the game.”</p>

entries.title: Defensores con drones denuncian coleaderos en los suburbios de Illinois por maltrato animal
entries.summary: <p>Un hombre a caballo en un corral cabalga frenéticamente junto a un toro que huye, alcanzando la cola del animal y envolviéndola rápida pero hábilmente alrededor de su bota derecha, manteniéndola agarrada.</p><p>Como se pretendía, la maniobra hace que el toro gire y caiga al polvo.</p><p>El jinete —parte de un “jaripeo en un patio trasero” el verano pasado en las afueras del noroeste— galopa alejándose, sosteniendo en la mano algo grotesco: parte de la cola del toro, arrancada.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-810000" name="module-810000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Llamada “degloving” (lesión por despegamiento de la piel), la lesión es común en este tipo de eventos, según activistas locales por los derechos de los animales que llevan años tratando de detener el coleadero en Illinois, quienes afirman que equivale a un abuso animal que claramente es ilegal bajo la ley estatal, aunque la policía local y los fiscales no lo hacen cumplir lo suficiente, dicen.</p><p>Una excepción es el Condado de McHenry, donde tres hombres fueron sentenciados el miércoles a un año de libertad condicional, parecido a la libertad vigilada, por cargos de crueldad animal relacionados con el evento del verano pasado en la zona no incorporada de Woodstock. Impuesta por el juez Justin Hansen, la sentencia incluyó multas de $250 y prohibió a los hombres el “contacto intencional” con animales, con algunas excepciones, durante ese periodo.</p><p>Los hombres fueron procesados, al menos en parte, con base en imágenes de dron del jaripeo tomadas por el grupo de defensa animal, SHARK, cuyas siglas en inglés significan "Showing Animals Respect and Kindness" (Mostrando Amabilidad y Respeto a los Animales). La organización ha documentado eventos similares en el extremo sur del Condado de Will y en áreas fuera del norte del estado, incluido el Condado de Ogle.</p><p>Los registros de la corte dicen que uno de los hombres en el Condado de McHenry, Alfredo Magallanes, “participó en un evento de coleadero de jaripeo” en el que “con conocimiento jaló la cola de un toro vivo con suficiente fuerza como para provocar una lesión por desprendimiento de la piel que fue captada en video por dron”.</p><p>“El acto causó dolor y expuso al animal a mayor daño e infección, constituyendo un trato cruel hacia el toro, contrario” a la ley estatal.</p><p>Magallanes, de 24 años y residente de Marengo, se declaró culpable, al igual que otros dos hombres con cargos similares, según muestran los registros.</p><p>Cada uno se disculpó en la corte el miércoles y describió las lesiones en las colas como no intencionales, y su abogado Garrett Fisher le dijo a Hansen: “Todos estos fueron eventos accidentales”, en lo que es “un deporte muy físico y exigente” que “de ninguna manera recompensa ni fomenta” hacerles daño a los animales.</p><p>El fiscal Joe Creager respondió, “Llamar a esto un deporte o incluso un deporte exigente es una ofensa al rodeo… esto es castigar a las vacas por deporte”.</p><p>Un menor de Lockport también fue citado inicialmente, pero su caso fue desestimado.</p><p>Una quinta persona, Socorro Barrientos, de 68 años, ya fue llevada a juicio, pero un juez aún no ha dictado veredicto, según los registros de la corte, que indicaba que la acusada pateó “a un toro en la cabeza más de 10 veces” en el mismo evento que los demás “mientras estaba en el suelo y no representaba una amenaza”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>En una escena captada en video por un grupo de defensa de los animales con un dron en el Condado de McHenry el año pasado, un hombre a caballo persigue a un novillo, le agarra y le arranca la cola, y el animal se aleja cojeando.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Showing Animals Respect and Kindness</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Jodie Wiederkehr, residente de Chicago y directora de campañas de SHARK, no cree que el coleadero y los jaripeos en propiedad privada estén necesariamente volviéndose más comunes en la región, sino que se les presta más atención porque los activistas están destacando el maltrato que a menudo ocurre.</p><p>“La razón por la que sucede es que se está ganando mucho dinero”, dice Wiederkehr, y señala que los boletos para asistir a los eventos privados pueden costar $50 cada uno y que se diseñan para ser festivos, con “baile, bebidas y diversión”, además de las exhibiciones de rodeo.</p><p>Dice que el trato a los toros equivale a tortura, incluso cuando no se les arrancan las colas.</p><p>Otro video de SHARK de un jaripeo allí muestra a un toro cojeando, con lo que parece ser una pata rota, tras ser derribado por un jinete a caballo.</p><p>Wiederkehr dice que a veces los animales son pinchados o golpeados con palos, electrocutados con una vara eléctrica para ganado, trabajados hasta el agotamiento e incluso mordidos en la cola por participantes del jaripeo, en un aparente intento de estimular a las criaturas.</p><p>“Estos animales a menudo se quedan sufriendo durante horas sin tratamiento veterinario ni alivio del dolor”, dice Wiederkehr, quien jugó un papel clave para que el Concejo Municipal votara en 2020 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2020/3/11/21175331/horse-drawn-carriages-ban-chicago-brendan-reilly-brian-hopkins" target="_blank" >a favor de prohibir los carruajes jalados por caballos en Chicago</a> debido a preocupaciones por su bienestar.</p><p>Wiederkehr tuvo problemas en el Condado de Ogle el año pasado por hacer llamadas reportando abuso animal en el lugar y, al no quedar satisfecha con que no iban a enviar a la policía, reportó un tiroteo en un aparente intento de forzar una respuesta.</p><p>Fue condenada el mes pasado por denuncia falsa y acoso, pero aún no ha sido sentenciada.</p><p>Su abogado está solicitando un nuevo juicio.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-credit"><p>Proporcionada</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>La Ley de Cuidado Humano de los Animales de Illinois dice: “Ninguna persona o propietario podrá golpear, tratar cruelmente, atormentar, dejar de alimentar, sobrecargar de trabajo o abusar de cualquier otro modo de un animal”.</p><p>Los dueños de animales deben proporcionar “atención veterinaria cuando sea necesaria para prevenir el sufrimiento”.</p><p>Steve Hindi, presidente de SHARK y con base en el Condado de Kane, dijo que con demasiada frecuencia las autoridades en Illinois no hacen cumplir la ley, incluso ante evidencia clara.</p><p>Un argumento que ha escuchado el grupo de Hindi: el estatuto no prohíbe específicamente el coleadero.</p><p>A lo que Hindi responde, “No existe una ley que explícitamente diga que no puedes arrojar a un cachorro por una ventana”, pero el estatuto contra la crueldad lo cubriría claramente.</p><p>“No deberíamos necesitar una ley nueva”, dice.</p><p>Aun así, una propuesta de ley fue presentada por la senadora estatal Rachel Ventura (demócrata por Joliet) en la Asamblea General el año pasado para prohibir específicamente el coleadero. La medida decía en parte: “Ninguna persona podrá arrastrar o jalar intencionalmente a cualquier bovino por su cola por cualquier medio con el propósito de entretenimiento, deporte, práctica o concurso”.</p><p>Coprotagonizada por el senador estatal, Li Arellano Jr. (republicano por Dixon), la iniciativa no avanzó este año. En cambio, en el Senado de Illinois se aprobó una resolución no vinculante que desaprobaba el coleadero, diciendo “desalentamos todos los actos de coleadero bovino y los daños asociados”.</p><p>Ha habido cierta resistencia a endurecer las medidas contra el coleadero, debido a su lugar en la cultura del jaripeo mexicano, que se remonta a siglos atrás.</p><p>Arellano dice que eso no cambia el hecho de que “la tasa de lesiones es más alta que en casi cualquier otro evento de jaripeo”, y que no conoce ninguna organización de rodeo estadounidense de buena reputación que actualmente promueva el coleadero, ya sea en eventos estilo mexicano o en los rodeos estilo western más comunes en Estados Unidos.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop="">
